limitations: No limitations section anywhere in the paper; the authors concede only that the excess of grade 3 or 4 abnormal liver function in the gemcitabine-alone arm was possibly a result of inferior disease control and biliary drainage, and that until ABC-01 and this trial the evidence base was non-randomised phase 2 studies
critique: The trial is a continuation of ABC-01, and the 86 patients randomised there generated the progression-free survival signal used to justify the extension and were then counted in this 410-patient confirmatory analysis, so the hypothesis and the test of it share data

Median follow-up was 8.2 months, shorter than the 11.7-month median survival being reported; the numbers at risk fall to 17 against 4 by 24 months and 2 against 2 by 32 months, so nothing beyond two years is estimable

Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is 80 of 410 patients and no site-specific hazard ratio is reported; the forest plot showing no heterogeneity is used to license pooling in a trial with no power to detect site-by-treatment interaction

Gallbladder cancer is 36% of the population and ampullary carcinoma a further 5%, so more than two-fifths of the evidence for the iCCA standard of care comes from tumours of different origin and different biology

The two arms differ in gemcitabine schedule as well as in cisplatin, 1000 mg/m2 on days 1 and 8 of 21 against days 1, 8 and 15 of 28, so the comparison is regimen against regimen and cannot isolate the contribution of adding cisplatin

Objective response was assessable in only 303 of 410 patients because measurable disease was not required at entry, and the 81.4% versus 71.8% tumour control rate at P = 0.049 is computed on that incomplete subset and counts stable disease as control

Imaging was obtained only at weeks 12 and 24 by RECIST 1.0 with no confirmatory scan, so progression-free survival can only move in 12-week steps and the 3-month difference in median progression-free survival is of the same order as the assessment interval

Biliary obstruction was deliberately not counted as progression, which in a disease whose dominant local event is biliary obstruction removes a clinically meaningful progression event from the primary biological endpoint's companion measure

Only 72 of 410 patients (18%) received any second-line therapy, so the overall survival difference was generated in a setting with almost no post-progression treatment and will not transfer to current practice

Treatment duration differed substantially between arms, 21 against 14 weeks, P = 0.003, and 63% against 52% started a second 12 weeks, so the arms also differ in total exposure and in contact with the treating team
The explanation offered for better liver function tests on the combination, superior disease control and biliary drainage, is an interpretation with no drainage-procedure data reported to support it
Lilly Oncology supplied gemcitabine free and gave an unrestricted educational grant to a trial in which both arms receive Lilly's drug and the result establishes a gemcitabine-containing standard
The trial was open-label with investigator-assessed progression and no blinded central review of imaging is described
No tissue collection, molecular stratification or biobanking is described, so the trial that defined the control arm for every subsequent biliary trial left no material to characterise who benefited

Two letters in the New England Journal of Medicine (Hall, PMID 20653076, with the authors' reply; Cariati, PMID 20647216) questioned the cost-benefit of a 3.6-month median gain; both were identified from the citation record and not read here
20375404.n: 410 patients with locally advanced or metastatic biliary tract cancer at 37 UK centres, of whom 80 (20%) had intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, 149 gallbladder cancer, 73 extrahepatic and 57 hilar cholangiocarcinoma, 20 ampullary cancer and 31 unspecified; 86 of the 410 came from the preceding randomised phase 2 ABC-01 study
20375404.bottom_line: ABC-02 established cisplatin plus gemcitabine as first-line treatment for advanced biliary tract cancer, with median survival of 11.7 against 8.1 months and a hazard ratio of 0.64 (0.52-0.80) at no cost in overall toxicity. It does not establish a benefit in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma specifically, since iCCA was 80 of 410 patients and no site-specific estimate was ever reported. Median follow-up was 8.2 months, shorter than the median survival it reports, and 86 of the patients came from the phase 2 study that generated the hypothesis.
20375404.funding: Supported by University College London Hospitals and UCL Comprehensive Biomedical Research Centre, Cancer Research UK, and an unrestricted educational grant from Lilly Oncology, which supplied gemcitabine free of charge and had no role in accrual, analysis, interpretation or writing

limitations: The sample size is small because intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is less common than the cancers for which chemoembolisation has a more established role
There may have been biases in referral for treatment, so the results may not represent all patients with unresectable intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma
Treatment was customised to each patient, with varying sequences of surgery, ablation, systemic and radiation therapy
The authors concede that comparison with published systemic therapy series is not possible because those series mixed in Klatskin, ampullary and gallbladder tumours with different prognosis
They accept that RECIST diameter criteria understate response because chemoembolisation produces necrosis without shrinkage
critique: 40% of the cohort, 25 of 62, had adenocarcinoma of unknown primary rather than proven cholangiocarcinoma, and these patients are kept in the survival analysis on the strength of a non-significant comparison, P = .88, in a sample with no power to show a difference

17 of 62 patients (27%) had no evaluable imaging follow-up, so the 76% local disease control figure is computed on 45 patients and the missing 17 are the ones most likely to have progressed or died early

Survival is reported from two different origins, 20 months from diagnosis and 15 months from first chemoembolisation, and the more favourable figure is the one that enters the literature; the gap between them is the lead time before referral

The 28-month against 16-month survival advantage in patients who also received systemic chemotherapy, HR 1.94 (1.13-3.33), P = .02, is a comparison of 18 fitter patients chosen by their own oncologists against 44 others, and it is reported as a treatment finding
Local disease control of 76% is 64% stable disease and only 11% partial response, so the headline control figure is mostly absence of measured growth over a short interval
Median time to progression anywhere was 8 months with 28% progression-free at 12 months, which is the number that bounds the treatment and is not in the paper's conclusion
Extrahepatic disease at the time of chemoembolisation was not excluded and is reported as non-prognostic at P = .12 in a sample where that interval, 0.35 to 1.20, easily contains a large effect
11% had a prior hepatectomy and others had ablation or radiation, so the cohort mixes first-line and salvage treatment with no separate analysis
The two centres contributed 40 and 22 patients with no centre-level comparison of response or survival reported, although an identical protocol is the paper's stated basis for pooling them

The regimen is historical: an ethiodol and polyvinyl alcohol emulsion of cisplatin, doxorubicin and mitomycin predates drug-eluting beads, yttrium-90 radioembolisation and gemcitabine-cisplatin as first-line standard, and the cohort was treated before FGFR2 or IDH1 testing existed

The in-text reference numbering for the RECIST and ECOG citations is transposed in the published PDF, so the stated response and performance criteria cannot be traced to their sources from the text as printed
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed, so no independent published appraisal accompanies the series
21425151.n: 62 patients with unresectable intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma treated with an identical conventional chemoembolisation protocol at two US centres, 40 at the University of Pennsylvania and 22 at the Medical College of Wisconsin, across 165 procedures; 37 had biopsy-proven cholangiocarcinoma and 25 had intrahepatic adenocarcinoma of unknown primary of pancreaticobiliary type, with a median dominant mass of 7.8 cm
21425151.bottom_line: This two-centre series is the reference safety dataset for conventional chemoembolisation in iCCA: major complications after 5 of 165 procedures, no 30-day disease-specific mortality, a one-day median stay and stable performance status in 82%, with 20 months median survival from diagnosis. It cannot establish efficacy, having no control arm, 40% of patients with adenocarcinoma of unknown primary, 27% without evaluable imaging and a treatment course individualised with surgery, ablation and radiation. Time to progression was 8 months, and the regimen itself predates every current alternative.
21425151.funding: No funding statement; the authors made no disclosures

limitations: The study has the limitations inherent to any retrospective design and cannot fully account for biases a randomised study would address
Selection bias could have favoured patients who received higher radiation doses, although the authors state they found no evidence of it
Treatment-related toxicity may have been underestimated because it was captured only from the medical record
The variety of dose and fractionation schedules used, 35 to 100 Gy in 3 to 30 fractions, may be viewed as a limitation, which the authors defend as common in the liver literature
critique: The dose threshold that gives the paper its title, a biologic equivalent dose of 80.5 Gy, is the median of the cohort's own dose distribution, so the comparison is a data-derived split of 19 patients against 60 rather than a prespecified threshold

Dose is inseparable from era and technique: the high doses arrived after 2010 together with breath-hold gating and daily diagnostic-quality CT guidance, and patients treated after 2010 survived 50 against 24 months, p = .007, which is the same signal reported twice

The high-dose group had significantly smaller planning target volumes, median 415 against 614 cm3, p = .02, so the patients who got more dose had more favourable anatomy, which is exactly the selection the authors say they found no evidence of

Survival is reported from diagnosis, median 30 months, in a cohort where 89% had chemotherapy before radiotherapy, so the clock starts before a selection step that removed everyone who progressed during chemotherapy

Whole-cohort local control falls from 81% at 1 year to 45% at 2 and 27% at 3, and 48% of patients had primary tumour progression with 89% of those inside the high-dose region, so the ablative claim is not supported by the cohort's own failure pattern

Median progression-free survival is reported as 30 months, the same as median overall survival, which is not coherent with 51% developing new intrahepatic metastases and 41% extrahepatic disease, and the definition reconciling these is not given

The multivariable hazard ratios for biologic equivalent dose, 0.96 (0.94-0.98) for local control and 0.97 (0.95-0.99) for survival, are per-unit-dose effects fitted to 79 patients with a dose range of 35 to 100 Gy, and tumour size, satellite lesions, performance status and CA 19-9 all came out non-significant, which in a cohort this size means the model had little power to adjust for anything

Toxicity is reported as no radiation-induced liver disease and no liver failure without tumour progression, a formulation that excludes the deaths most likely to be dose-related: 32 of 36 deaths with a known cause were from intrahepatic progression through biliary or vascular complications, and the paper does not separate those from radiation injury

9% developed biliary stenosis needing a stent at a median of 10 months and 4 of those 7 also had tumour progression, so biliary toxicity and progression are confounded in exactly the patients where dose matters

Single biologic equivalent dose conversion with an assumed alpha-beta ratio is used to equate 3-fraction and 30-fraction schedules; the whole dose-response analysis depends on that model and no sensitivity analysis across alpha-beta values is presented
59% of the cohort was stage IV, so more than half the patients had disease that no amount of local dose could control, and they are included in the survival analysis that supports dose escalation

Brade and Dawson's accompanying editorial (J Clin Oncol 2016;34:203-4, PMID 26644540) raises whether retrospective dose-response data in a rare cancer should change practice without a randomised trial; it was identified from the citation record and not read here
26503201.n: 79 consecutive patients with inoperable intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma treated with definitive-intent radiotherapy at a single institution between 2002 and 2014, median tumour size 7.9 cm (2.2 to 17), 59% stage IV, 89% having had chemotherapy first; 19 received a biologic equivalent dose above 80.5 Gy and 60 below it
26503201.bottom_line: This 79-patient single-centre series is the origin of the ablative-dose argument in inoperable iCCA, reporting 3-year survival of 73% above a biologic equivalent dose of 80.5 Gy against 38% below, with dose the only independent predictor of local control and survival. It cannot separate dose from era, technique and target volume: the high-dose patients were treated after 2010 with breath-hold gating and image guidance and had significantly smaller targets. Only 19 patients received the high dose, the threshold is the cohort's own median, and local control still fell to 27% at three years.
26503201.funding: No funding statement in the paper; author disclosures are posted online rather than printed, and the article lists clinical trial information NCT02200042 although the analysis is retrospective

limitations: The intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma cohort was enrolled in parallel with no efficacy hypothesis, only for precision of estimates, so the powered endpoint applies to the hepatocellular cohort

The authors recognise the limitations of the linear-quadratic model in comparing their 15-fraction schedule with the 6-fraction Princess Margaret schedule, and note the median doses differ substantially in 2-Gy equivalents, 67 Gy against 48 Gy
They concede that part of the difference in local control may relate to the fractionation schedule used rather than to protons

They attribute part of the overall survival difference from the Princess Margaret study to the effect of protons versus photons on post-treatment hepatic function, an inference rather than a measurement
They acknowledge that the comparison with the ABC-02 gemcitabine-cisplatin median of 11.7 months is confounded because only 27% of ABC-02 patients had locally advanced disease
critique: The 94.1% 2-year local control figure quoted for iCCA is measured at a landmark the disease then crosses: four further local failures occurred beyond 24 months, for six in 39 patients, while median follow-up among survivors was only 19.5 months, so the headline is a snapshot taken before the failures arrived

Local control was scored by RECIST 1.0 size criteria with progression determined by the interpreting radiologist and confirmed by the treating physician, with no central review; size criteria systematically overstate control after ablative radiation because treated tumours do not shrink

Median delivered dose was 58.0 GyE against an intended maximum of 67.5 GyE, and all eight local progressions occurred below 60 GyE, so the trial does not establish the dose its own data imply is needed

Distant failure dominated in the iCCA cohort, 21 of 39 (53.8%) with metastases and only 8 of 39 (20.5%) alive without progression, which means local control in this histology bought little and the paper's primary measure is the one least relevant to outcome

The 22-month median survival has a confidence interval of 12.4 to 49.7 months in 39 patients, an interval too wide to compare with any other series, yet it is set against ABC-02's 11.7 months in the discussion

The vascular thrombosis hazard ratio of 3.615 (1.303-10.025) comes from 11 affected patients, so the only significant prognostic finding rests on a handful of events with an interval spanning nearly an order of magnitude

Dose was de-escalated as needed to keep mean uninvolved liver dose at or below 24 GyE, so dose was assigned by anatomy; patients with more favourable anatomy received more dose, which confounds the dose-outcome relationship the discussion relies on
Two of the 39 iCCA patients had mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma tumours and are counted in the cohort, a histology excluded from most iCCA series

Proton therapy was available only at the three participating centres, so nothing in the trial addresses whether the same schedule delivered with photons would give the same result; the randomised answer was deferred to NRG GI-001, which later closed early for poor accrual
61.5% had received previous chemotherapy with no analysis by prior treatment, so the cohort mixes first-line and salvage radiation

The 4.8% grade 3 toxicity rate is based on radiation-related events in 83 patients across two histologies, and the iCCA-specific rate is 7.7%, three patients, of which one was liver failure with ascites; a toxicity claim at that denominator cannot exclude a clinically meaningful rate
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed, so no independent published appraisal accompanies the result
26668346.n: 83 evaluable patients of 92 consented at Massachusetts General Hospital, MD Anderson and the University of Pennsylvania between November 2009 and February 2015, comprising 44 with hepatocellular carcinoma and 39 with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (37 pure plus 2 mixed); the iCCA cohort had a median longest tumour dimension of 6.0 cm (2.2 to 10.9), 89.7% without cirrhosis and 61.5% previously treated with chemotherapy
26668346.bottom_line: This multi-institutional phase 2 trial shows that 15-fraction high-dose proton therapy can be delivered to large liver tumours with 4.8% grade 3 toxicity and almost no decline in liver function, and reports 94.1% 2-year local control and 22.5 months median survival in its 39 iCCA patients. The iCCA cohort had no efficacy hypothesis, no control arm and no central review, so none of that is evidence of a survival benefit. Local failures kept accruing past the two-year landmark, and 54% of iCCA patients developed distant metastases, so local control was not what limited them.
26668346.funding: Supported by National Institutes of Health grant 2P01CA021239-29A1 and in part by a Cancer Clinical Investigator Team Leadership Award from the National Cancer Institute through a supplement to grant P30CA006516; author disclosures are posted online rather than printed

limitations: The study is retrospective and single-institution, the former with obvious implications for selection bias and the latter precluding generalisability pending a multicentre study
A significant proportion of the hepatic arterial infusion patients, 44 of 93, came from two clinical trials, which the authors say somewhat limits generalisability
The heterogeneity of systemic regimens, inherent to studies outside controlled trials, is a limitation that must be considered when interpreting the results
Potential differences in staging may have existed between the groups because not all patients were staged surgically, mitigated only by serial scanning of equivocal radiological findings
critique: Treatment assignment was made by the treating medical oncologist with no matching, no propensity adjustment and no multivariable survival model reported for the main comparison, so a 12.4-month median survival difference is attributed to the pump on the strength of a log-rank P value alone

All hepatic arterial infusion patients were surgically explored and staged at operation whereas only 42% of the systemic-alone group were, so the groups were staged by different methods and stage migration alone could produce the observed difference
The control group for the liver-confined comparison is 26 patients, of whom only about 30% received gemcitabine-cisplatin, so the comparator is a mixture of regimens including several no longer used
The most favourable comparison, 30.8 against 15 months, is made against 9 patients who received a modern doublet, a denominator too small to support the number it generates
Six patients in the infusion group received hepatic arterial infusion alone because they could not tolerate systemic therapy, so the groups are not even consistent in what they received

Response data were available for 79 of 93 infusion patients and 18 of 74 systemic-alone patients, so the response comparison of 59% against 39% is drawn from a quarter of the control arm; the text also gives the infusion denominator as 78 in one place and 79 in another

Progression-free survival, the endpoint least affected by subsequent treatment, showed no significant difference, 12 against 7 months, P = .2, and neither did response, P = .11; only overall survival separated, which is the endpoint most vulnerable to the selection the design cannot control

No pump complication rate, no biliary toxicity rate and no treatment-related mortality are reported anywhere in this paper, with the reader referred to earlier publications, so the procedural risk cannot be weighed against the survival claim from this source

Only 8 of 236 patients (3%) converted to resection, of whom 2 died perioperatively and 5 recurred within a year, with negative margins in 5 of 8; the conversion result is presented as encouraging when two of eight patients died of the operation

44 of 93 infusion patients came from two prospective trials and were therefore subject to trial eligibility criteria, while the comparator group was not, so trial-grade fitness is built into one arm of a retrospective comparison
The paper asserts that the results represent the best reported treatment results for advanced intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, a cross-literature claim from a single-centre retrospective series
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed, so no independent published appraisal accompanies the survival claim
26695839.n: 236 patients with unresectable intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and complete data, drawn from 525 biopsy-confirmed cases evaluated at Memorial Sloan Kettering between January 2000 and August 2012; the analysis focuses on the 167 without distant metastases, of whom 104 had liver-confined disease, comparing 93 who had hepatic arterial infusion plus systemic chemotherapy with 74 who had systemic chemotherapy alone
26695839.bottom_line: In 167 patients with unresectable iCCA without distant metastases, adding hepatic arterial infusion floxuridine to systemic chemotherapy was associated with median survival of 30.8 against 18.4 months in liver-confined disease, the largest such series available and the basis for referring these patients to pump centres. It cannot show the pump caused that difference: assignment was by oncologist preference, all infusion patients were surgically staged against 42% of controls, 44 of 93 came from trials, and neither response nor progression-free survival differed significantly. Conversion to resection happened in 3%, with two perioperative deaths among eight.
26695839.funding: Supported by the National Institutes of Health / National Cancer Institute Cancer Center Support grant P30 CA008748; individual authors report personal fees from Baxter, Amgen, Medtronic, Johnson and Johnson, Ipsen and others outside the submitted work

limitations: The number of patients analysed is still modest, especially in the very early iCCA group of interest, and 47% of those were incidental findings
The pathological diagnosis of iCCA at the different centres cannot be confirmed because external review was possible in only 70% of cases
Each centre had its own pathologist analyse the explant because of the retrospective design, which may have led to tumour number and size being understaged
This is a retrospective study with all the limitations of such a design
Univariate and multivariate analyses were performed as exploratory analyses only, on variables chosen for clinical significance

Information on positive lymph nodes and lymphovascular invasion, both recurrence risk factors after resection, was scarce because these patients were not thought to have iCCA and so were not staged for it

The intermediate category of patients in Supporting Fig. S1 held too few cases to support a robust opinion, and the single 2.1-3 cm result is difficult to interpret because of the small number of patients
A prospective multicentre clinical trial is needed to confirm the results
critique: The study group is defined by the explant, so patients who were listed with an undiagnosed iCCA and then dropped off the waiting list for progression never enter the denominator; the 93%, 84% and 65% survival figures are conditional on having reached transplantation and are not an intention-to-treat estimate for a 2 cm iCCA

81 iCCA were found in 25,016 transplants and only 48 of those had iCCA alone, of whom 15 were very early; the headline therefore rests on 0.06% of the transplant denominator, and the 33 patients with a concomitant HCC nodule were moved into a separate table rather than analysed with them

Cumulative recurrence is 18% at both 3 and 5 years in the very early group, which means no recurrence was observed after 3 years in a group of 15 with 2 events in total; no numbers at risk are given at any time point, so the 5-year estimate cannot be judged

Follow-up was not comparable between the compared groups, 57.3 months (23.4-104.5) for very early versus 24.7 months (12.7-63.4) for advanced, P = 0.04, yet the two survival curves are read against each other as if observation were equivalent

The multivariable Cox model was fitted on 36 patients with roughly 20 recurrence events across the whole cohort, and the resulting hazard ratios of 4.7 (1.6-13.8) and 6.1 (1.9-20.2) have intervals spanning an order of magnitude, which is a model with more parameters than the event count supports

Four patients listed beyond the UCSF criteria were kept in the cohort on the stated grounds that the analysis was exploratory, while being out of UCSF criteria was itself a significant univariate predictor of recurrence, HR 4.0 (1.6-10), P = 0.003

The 2.1-3 cm, not poorly differentiated subgroup that is the paper's only evidence above 2 cm has six patients and was defined after the outcomes were known; its P = 0.03 is a post hoc subgroup comparison, and the 3 cm transplant ceiling later attributed to this paper has no prospective basis in it

No period of disease stability and no neoadjuvant protocol were required or tested anywhere in the study, so the six-month stability rule that is sometimes cited to this paper is not something it examined

Mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma within the same nodule was an explicit exclusion, so the results cannot be extended to mixed tumours, and the paper's own discussion of mixed HCC-CCA survival is taken from other series

Bridging transarterial chemoembolisation, ablation or ethanol injection was permitted and is listed as a covariate, so some nodules measured at 2 cm or less on explant may have been larger before treatment; the proportion of very early patients who had bridging therapy is not reported separately

The resection comparison is to a historical literature range of 15% to 45% 5-year survival rather than to resected patients from the same 17 centres over the same period, so the claim that transplantation is competitive is not tested against a concurrent comparator
Table 1 gives advanced-group recurrence as 17 of 33 (51.5%) while the Results text gives 18 of 33 (54.5%), both attached to the same P = 0.006, and the discrepancy is not reconciled

Published correspondence in Hepatology (Gupta and Gupta 2017; Gu, Jeong and Xia 2017) argued the selection criteria need refining, including by aetiology such as HBV-related iCCA; those letters were identified from the citation record and not read in full here
27481548.n: 15 patients with a single iCCA of 2 cm or less, identified on explant pathology among 81 iCCA found in 25,016 liver transplants performed at 17 centres between January 2000 and December 2013, and compared with 33 patients whose explant iCCA was larger or multifocal
27481548.bottom_line: Fifteen cirrhotic patients whose explant showed a single iCCA of 2 cm or less had 65% 5-year survival and 18% recurrence, enough to justify a prospective trial of transplantation in that narrow group. It does not show that such patients can be identified before transplantation, since every diagnosis was made on the explant, and it tests neither a 3 cm ceiling nor any requirement for a period of disease stability. The comparison group is 33 patients with larger or multifocal explant tumours followed for less than half as long, not a concurrent resection cohort.
27481548.funding: Supported by grants from the Instituto de Salud Carlos III (PI14/00962), the Italian Association for Cancer Research and the Swiss National Science Foundation (PP00P3_139021); CIBEREHD supported by the Instituto de Salud Carlos III; Mazzaferro is on the speakers' bureau for BTG

limitations: Recruitment was terminated before the planned 300 patients were reached, which may have led to an underpowered analysis; enrolment slowed after about 2009 because most patients wanted adjuvant chemotherapy

The authors calculate only a 2.8% probability that the result would have been statistically significant even if the expected 189 deaths had occurred, and conclude increasing to 300 patients would not have changed the result
They state that adjuvant therapy should not target all patients but should focus on high-risk features after resection
critique: The trial enrolled only perihilar and distal bile duct cancer, with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer excluded, so a negative adjuvant result here cannot be carried to resected iCCA, which is how this trial is often cited

The 2.8% figure the authors use to dismiss underpowering is a conditional calculation made after the observed curves were known; it answers whether this result would have changed, not whether the trial could have detected a true moderate effect

Observed 5-year survival in the control arm was about 50% against an assumed 30%, because R2 resections, distant metastases, severe surgical complications, in-hospital deaths and gallbladder cancer were all excluded, so the trial tested adjuvant therapy in the patients least likely to need it

Only 61 of 117 (52.1%) completed protocol therapy and the median relative dose intensity was 82.2%, so the negative result is a test of gemcitabine as delivered to half the arm rather than of the intended regimen
The trial was open-label with no placebo, and recurrence was ascertained without a described blinded review, in a design where the observation arm had no scheduled treatment contact

Grade 3 or 4 neutropenia occurred in 58.4% against 3.8% and leucopenia in 29.2% against 1.9%, so the arms were trivially distinguishable to investigators and patients despite the survival curves overlapping

Subgroup P values are reported for node-positive, node-negative, R0 and R1 strata, each far from significance, and 3-year survival was numerically worse with gemcitabine in node-positive patients, yet the discussion still recommends targeting high-risk features with adjuvant therapy
Eli Lilly Japan, which markets gemcitabine, part-funded a trial of gemcitabine; the authors declare no conflict of interest, which sits oddly with the funding statement on the same page
The comparator is observation, not the oral fluoropyrimidine that BILCAP and ASCOT later supported, so the trial cannot inform the choice a surgeon actually faces today

48.9% of patients had a hepatectomy and 15.5% a portal vein resection, so the cohort mixes two very different operations with different recovery trajectories and no stratification or separate analysis by operation type for the primary endpoint
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed, so no independent published appraisal accompanies the result
29405274.n: 225 patients analysed of 226 randomised at 48 Japanese hospitals between 2007 and 2011 after macroscopically curative resection of extrahepatic bile duct cancer, 117 gemcitabine and 108 observation, comprising 102 perihilar and 123 distal tumours; intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma was not eligible
29405274.bottom_line: BCAT is a clean negative adjuvant trial: gemcitabine after resection of extrahepatic bile duct cancer gave a hazard ratio of 1.01 (0.70-1.45) for survival and 0.93 for relapse-free survival, with no subgroup benefiting and 58% grade 3-4 neutropenia. It says nothing about intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, which was ineligible, and nothing about the oral fluoropyrimidines now used. Its control arm did far better than assumed, 51.6% 5-year survival against an assumed 30%, because the enrolment criteria excluded nearly everyone at real risk.
29405274.funding: Supported by the Nagoya Surgery Support Organization and Eli Lilly Japan K.K., stated to have had no role in design, data collection, analysis or interpretation; the authors declare no conflict of interest

limitations: The rarity of iCCA together with the stringent requirement for long-term disease stability meant only nine patients were listed over a six-year period
No MELD exception was available, so finding organs was difficult and discarded or extended-criteria livers were often used
Regimens after initial gemcitabine-based therapy were heterogeneous because of the median 26 months between diagnosis and transplantation, reflecting an absence of standard in this setting
The small sample size limited statistical analysis, and larger prospective studies will be needed to validate the results
Resectability was determined solely by the surgeon members of the collaborative committee, which the authors state carried potential for bias
Patients were not randomised and were treated under a centre-approved clinical policy, so the study did not qualify for registration as a clinical trial
A clear-cut tumour size cut-off for transplant candidacy cannot be drawn from these results and a larger cohort will be needed

The authors concede that perihilar biopsy and portal lymphadenectomy during the exploratory part of the hepatectomy would be needed to avoid transplanting patients with occult disease, having found two patients with extrahepatic metastases called stable before transplant and one with perihilar fat invasion found only on explant
critique: Survival is computed only on the six patients who reached transplantation; the nine referrals never accepted and the three listed patients still waiting at censoring are outside the denominator, so the paper reports no intention-to-treat result for the strategy it proposes

Overall survival of 100% with a 95% confidence interval of 100-100 at 1 year reflects zero deaths among six patients rather than any precision, and the 83.3% figure at 3 and 5 years rests on a single death with an interval of 27.3-97.5
Recurrence-free survival is identical at 1, 3 and 5 years, 50% (11.1-80.4), because all three recurrences happened by 8.6 months; the 3 and 5-year values add no information beyond the first year

This is an interim analysis of an ongoing clinical management protocol censored on a date chosen by the investigators, with three of the twelve listed patients still on the waitlist, so the cohort is not closed and the denominator can change with the next cut

Median pre-transplant cumulative tumour diameter was 14.2 cm and no patient was below 5 cm, so the series contains no information about the small tumours to which its six-month stability rule is now routinely applied

Two of six recipients had lesions described as stable on pre-transplant imaging, a bony lesion and subcentimetre lung nodules, that turned out to be metastases, meaning a third of the cohort was transplanted with the extrahepatic disease the entry criteria excluded

The genomic observations are four single patients: FGFR2 alterations in two who did not recur, KRAS in one who did and BAP1 in one who did, and from this the discussion speculates that another 10-20% of patients with favourable genetics might benefit

Three of the six grafts were extended-criteria orphan livers refused by every other centre and two were domino living-donor grafts, so only one recipient received a standard deceased-donor organ and the approach cannot be reproduced where such grafts are not available

Entry allowed either biopsy-proven malignancy or a CA19-9 above 100 U/mL, so a patient could be listed without tissue confirmation of cholangiocarcinoma, while the paper's own inclusion list elsewhere states biopsy or cytology confirmation
Prior liver resection more than six months before listing was permitted, so the six patients mix de novo and post-resection recurrent disease without the paper reporting how many of each

The only comparator anywhere in the paper is the patients' own median progression-free survival of 8 months on first-line and 3 months on second-line therapy, which is not a survival comparison and cannot separate the effect of transplantation from the effect of selecting patients whose disease had already been stable for six months

Reported figures disagree between text and table: median postoperative stay is 8.5 days (IQR 6.0-10.0) in the text but 9 days (range 5-18) in Table 1, and median time from diagnosis to transplant is given with an IQR of 17-33 in the abstract but 10-36 in Table 1
29548617.n: 6 patients with locally advanced unresectable intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma transplanted at a single centre, drawn from 12 accepted and listed out of 21 referred between 1 January 2010 and 1 December 2017
29548617.bottom_line: Six highly selected patients with bulky unresectable iCCA who had been radiographically stable for at least six months on chemotherapy survived transplantation well, with one death and three recurrences over a median 36 months. It does not show that transplantation beats continued chemotherapy, because there is no comparator and no intention-to-treat denominator: six of twenty-one referrals reached the operating room, and half the grafts were livers no other centre would take. The six-month stability rule it introduced is tested here only in tumours above 5 cm.
29548617.funding: No external funding; RTS reports support from Celgene, Eli Lilly, Agios, Codiak, Amgen and Halozyme outside the submitted work, and all other authors declare no competing interests

limitations: The planned hazard ratio of 0.60 was ambitious and the trial may have been underpowered, with only 126 relapse-free survival events
The median relapse-free survival fell on a plateau where the curves separate most, so the median is less representative of the true difference than the hazard ratio
No trend toward an overall survival benefit was seen, with a hazard ratio above 1, and the overall survival medians are likewise unrepresentative because of a plateau at the median

Chemotherapy given after relapse differed between the arms and may partly explain the discrepancy between a relapse-free survival trend and no overall survival benefit, supported by the trend toward lower post-relapse survival in the GEMOX arm
Other unknown factors might also explain the absence of an overall survival benefit
The authors treat the apparent harm in the gallbladder subgroup as a possible chance finding in a small group
critique: This is a negative trial on both co-primary endpoints: relapse-free survival HR 0.88 (0.62-1.25), P = .48, and time to definitive quality-of-life deterioration HR 1.28 (0.73-2.26), P = .39, and overall survival pointed the wrong way at HR 1.08 (0.70-1.66)

Post-relapse chemotherapy was grossly unbalanced, with 40 of 41 surveillance relapses receiving gemcitabine-based salvage against 9 of 33 after adjuvant GEMOX, so the overall survival comparison is between a group that got effective salvage and a group that largely did not; this is a design consequence of using the same drug class in the adjuvant arm

The iCCA subgroup of 86 patients, the largest primary site and the one this record is used for, has a relapse-free survival hazard ratio of 0.718 (0.431-1.196) and no overall survival estimate highlighted; the interval is wide enough to contain both a worthwhile benefit and harm

The gallbladder subgroup of 38 patients shows significant harm on both endpoints, relapse-free HR 2.559 (1.037-6.318) and overall survival HR 3.390 (1.169-9.830), reported without multiplicity adjustment across four primary sites, so it is as likely to be noise as the favourable iCCA point estimate is

The population is substantially lower risk than BILCAP's, 13% against 38% R1 and 38% against 47% node-positive, so the trial was a test of adjuvant therapy in patients with less residual disease to treat

Toxicity was severe and asymmetric, grade 3 events in 62% against 18% and grade 3 sensory neuropathy in 18%, with no benefit on either co-primary endpoint, so the trial delivered measurable harm for no measurable gain

The trial was open-label with surveillance as the comparator, and the quality-of-life co-primary endpoint was collected by questionnaire from unblinded patients who knew whether they were receiving chemotherapy

Four primary sites with different biology were pooled for feasibility and the trial was minimised but not powered by site, so neither the negative overall result nor any subgroup can be attributed to a particular tumour type

Multivariable predictors of relapse (R1, node-positive, microvascular invasion, CA 19-9 of 37 U/mL or more) are reported from the trial population as if prognostic findings, with no adjustment for the treatment arm interaction and no validation

No formal non-inferiority or futility boundary was prespecified, so a trial that cannot exclude an HR of 0.62 is reported as showing no benefit; the correct reading is that the question remains open for GEMOX at smaller effect sizes
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed, and the author disclosures are available only in a separate file at the DOI rather than printed with the paper
30707660.n: 196 patients randomised at 33 French centres within 3 months of R0 or R1 resection of biliary tract cancer, 194 analysed by intention to treat after two consent withdrawals; 86 of 194 (44%) were intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, 28% distal, 8% perihilar and 20% gallbladder, with 13% R1 and 38% node-positive
30707660.bottom_line: PRODIGE 12 is the negative adjuvant trial that removed gemcitabine-oxaliplatin from consideration after biliary resection: relapse-free survival HR 0.88 (0.62-1.25) with no quality-of-life benefit and overall survival numerically favouring surveillance. It does not establish that adjuvant therapy is useless, because it was powered for an HR of 0.60 in a low-risk population and the survival comparison is confounded by salvage chemotherapy given to 98% of surveillance relapses against 27% after GEMOX. Its 86 intrahepatic patients make it the most iCCA-weighted adjuvant trial available, with a subgroup interval of 0.431 to 1.196 that settles nothing.
30707660.funding: Supported by Programme Hospitalier de Recherche Clinique (PHRC 2009) and the Ligue Nationale Contre le Cancer, with no industry funding; most authors declare pharmaceutical consultancies in the separately posted disclosure file

limitations: The recruitment period ran about ten years, during which trial standards changed, so the 2005 protocol is open to criticism; in particular there was no fully defined statistical analysis plan when the study started
The heterogeneity of biliary tract cancers, both surgical and biological, makes an overall interpretation of the findings more complex
The surgical centre was not included in the modelling analyses adjusted for minimisation factors
The authors concede the trial was negative for the prespecified primary endpoint of overall survival by intention to treat, and argue from the data taken as a whole instead
There was no recurrence-free survival difference between 24 and 60 months, which the authors read as recurrence deferred rather than prevented
Quality-of-life differences, although statistically significant in places, were modest and unlikely to be clinically significant, and peripheral neuropathy scores should be read as hand-foot syndrome
critique: The primary endpoint failed, HR 0.81 (0.63-1.04), p = 0.097, and every positive number in the paper comes from either a covariate-adjusted sensitivity model or the per-protocol population; in an unblinded trial the per-protocol analysis reintroduces precisely the selection that randomisation existed to remove

The per-protocol population excluded patients who failed to complete even one cycle of capecitabine, so it is defined by tolerance of treatment, which tracks fitness and therefore survival; the 210 against 220 comparison is not a randomised contrast

The event target was cut from 270 to 234 by the data monitoring committee in July 2013 because events were accruing more slowly than assumed, which raised the detectable effect from HR 0.71 to 0.69 and left the trial with less power against the effect it was designed to find

Nodal status is one of the covariates that turns the sensitivity model positive, yet lymphadenectomy was not mandated for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, so the adjustment variable is ascertained less completely in exactly the subgroup to which this result is now applied

Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is 84 of 447 patients and no site-specific hazard ratio is reported anywhere, so the adjuvant standard for resected iCCA rests on 19% of a trial that was not powered for site

The recurrence-free survival hazard ratio is 0.75 (0.58-0.98) over the first 24 months and 1.48 (0.80-2.77) afterwards, which is a clear departure from proportional hazards; no test of the proportional hazards assumption is reported for the overall survival model whose single hazard ratio carries the conclusion

Adverse events for toxicity were not monitored in the observation group at all, so the 21% against 10% serious adverse event comparison is between a monitored arm and an unmonitored one and cannot be read as a between-group difference

Compliance was poor enough to matter: 55% completed all eight cycles, 46% required dose reduction and 32% stopped for toxicity, so the regimen as delivered differs substantially from the regimen as prescribed
The cost-effectiveness case is built on a mean QALY gain of 0.035 whose confidence interval (-0.034 to 0.104) includes both zero and net harm, in a trial that missed its primary endpoint

38% of patients had R1 resections and 47% were node-positive, a considerably higher-risk population than a typical resected iCCA, so the absolute survival difference does not transfer to a margin-negative, node-negative patient

The subgroup hazard ratios quoted for men, 0.70 (0.50-0.99), and poorly differentiated disease, 0.60 (0.39-0.93), have no significant heterogeneity test behind them and invite over-reading of who benefits

Roche funded the trial with an advisory role in its design, and Roche markets capecitabine; several authors declare Roche honoraria or research funding, which bears on a conclusion that defines Roche's drug as the standard of care

The authors state in their own key-messages box that the trial is 'uniquely placed to define the standard of care as capecitabine' and that another surveillance-controlled trial is unlikely to be done, a position that converts a failed primary endpoint into a practice standard by declaring the question closed

The linked comment by Malka and Edeline (Lancet Oncol 2019, PMID 30922732) asks whether this evidence suffices to define a standard of care; it was identified from the citation record and its arguments are not reproduced here
30922733.n: 447 patients randomised after curative-intent resection of biliary tract cancer at 44 UK specialist centres between March 2006 and December 2014, of whom 84 (19%) had intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, 128 hilar, 156 lower common bile duct and 79 muscle-invasive gallbladder cancer; 168 (38%) were R1 and 210 (47%) node-positive
30922733.bottom_line: BILCAP is the largest adjuvant trial in resected biliary tract cancer and is the reason capecitabine is offered after resection, with intention-to-treat median survival of 51.1 against 36.4 months. It did not meet its primary endpoint: HR 0.81 (0.63-1.04), p = 0.097, and the significant results come from a covariate-adjusted sensitivity model and from the per-protocol population of an unblinded trial. Only 19% of patients had intrahepatic disease and no site-specific estimate was reported, so the iCCA-specific benefit remains untested.
30922733.funding: Cancer Research UK and Roche; the funder had an advisory role in study design but no role in running the study, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing; several authors declare honoraria and research funding from Roche among many other companies, all stated to be outside the submitted work

limitations: Follow-up diagnostic pathology was available for only 66% of patients, which the authors attribute to most biliary malignancies being unresectable or the patients being poor surgical candidates

A separate bile duct specimen from the one used for pathological evaluation was used for sequencing in order to ensure sufficient DNA, which the authors say may explain incongruent results between the two modalities
The study does not address the optimal gene panel or the best approach to integrating sequencing into stricture evaluation
No single modality or combination reached 95% sensitivity without a loss of specificity
critique: A negative result does not exclude cancer and the paper does not lead with that: there were 37 false negatives (25%) and the negative predictive value is only 63%, so a clinician who stops at a negative BiliSeq is wrong a third of the time

In 12 of those false-negative cases the same panel found an alteration in the resected tumour, which means the failure was sampling or tumour cellularity below the 3% allele-frequency limit rather than tumour biology, and that failure mode is not quantifiable prospectively

Specificity of 100% is computed against a reference standard in which brushing cytology and negative biopsies were disallowed as evidence in either direction, and 34% of patients were adjudicated on clinical and radiographic course rather than tissue, a standard that cannot generate a false positive for a molecular test

The sequencing and the pathology were done on different specimens, so the central 73% against 48% sensitivity comparison is not a head-to-head test on the same material; the authors concede the specimen difference may explain discordance but still draw the comparison

The assay was run on a purpose-collected brush or biopsy placed directly into DNA lysis buffer in the laboratory that developed it, so nothing here addresses performance on residual CytoLyt or formalin-fixed material, where other groups report assay failure near 11%

The 28-gene panel does not detect FGFR2 fusions and omits chromatin remodelling genes such as ARID1A, which together occur in up to 20% of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas, so the panel misses the alterations that matter most for iCCA treatment while the paper's therapeutic yield is presented as 13%
The primary sclerosing cholangitis result, where the gain over cytology is largest at 83% against 8%, rests on 12 malignant cases with a confidence interval of 0.51 to 0.98
Only 38 of 252 strictures were intrahepatic, so the paper that is cited for molecular diagnosis of iCCA mostly studied extrahepatic and distal disease and reports no intrahepatic-specific sensitivity

The two trastuzumab responses are single cases treated concurrently with gemcitabine-cisplatin and followed for 8 and 12 months, so the shrinkage cannot be attributed to the targeted agent, yet they carry the paper's clinical-utility claim

Adding CA19-9 raises sensitivity to 95% at the cost of dropping specificity to 68%, which means roughly a third of benign strictures would be called malignant; that combination is presented alongside the others without stating that it is clinically unusable
The first author declares an honorarium from Foundation Medicine, a commercial sequencing provider, in a paper advocating routine sequencing of biliary specimens
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed, so no independent published appraisal accompanies the accuracy claims
30971436.n: 252 patients and 346 biliary specimens obtained at ERCP at a single centre, a 57-patient training cohort from September 2014 to April 2016 followed by a prospective validation cohort of 195 from September 2016 to August 2018; 220 had adequate follow-up for the accuracy analysis, 38 strictures were intrahepatic and 47 hilar, 22 patients had intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and 37 had primary sclerosing cholangitis
30971436.bottom_line: This is the study that put targeted sequencing of ERCP specimens into the work-up of an indeterminate biliary stricture, raising sensitivity for high-grade dysplasia or cancer from 48% with pathology to 73% alone and 83% combined, with specificity held at 99%. It does not make a negative test reassuring: a quarter of cancers were missed and the negative predictive value is 63%. Sequencing and pathology were run on different specimens, only 38 of 252 strictures were intrahepatic, and the panel does not detect FGFR2 fusions.
30971436.funding: Funded by the University of Pittsburgh Institute of Precision Medicine; the first author has received an honorarium from Foundation Medicine

limitations: The single-arm design made interpretation of the results difficult

Outcomes in locally advanced intrahepatic disease may have been better than in populations of all locally advanced or metastatic biliary tract cancers, so the comparison with those series is not like for like
The study was performed only in centres experienced with glass microspheres
SIRT doses were set from label instructions, while accumulating evidence suggests that defining the dose delivered to the tumour rather than a generic dose to the targeted liver might improve results
No data on molecular alterations were collected, although these might influence outcomes
The authors advise against SIRT with chemotherapy in patients with cirrhosis after hepatic failure occurred in 9 of 12 such patients, irreversibly in 5
critique: The primary endpoint is a 3-month response rate against a 22% futility threshold, which tests the regimen against a historical number rather than against chemotherapy alone, and the reported 39% is investigator-assessed with central review at 41% on best rather than 3-month response

Disease control of 98% (40 of 41) and a Choi response of 93% are reported alongside a RECIST response of 39%, so the headline figures depend entirely on which criterion is quoted and the paper quotes the most favourable in its abstract framing
Nine of 41 patients had major protocol deviations and 4 of 45 were excluded at the planning angiogram, so the 22% downstaging figure is drawn from a cohort selected before, during and after enrolment
The 22-month median survival has a confidence interval of 14 to 52 months, which the single-arm design cannot narrow and which overlaps almost every published series for this population

Hepatic failure occurred in 75% of cirrhotic patients and was irreversible in 5, all after whole-liver treatment; a safety signal of that magnitude in 12 patients means the trial cannot define a safe dose in cirrhosis, only that it harmed most of them

Grade 3 or 4 toxicity occurred in 71% of patients overall, including 5% acute hepatic failure and 7% ascites, which is a severe profile for a treatment whose benefit over chemotherapy alone is unmeasured

Delivered dose varied by more than an order of magnitude, 18 to 430 Gy to the targeted liver and 64 to 1673 Gy to tumour, so the trial does not describe a reproducible intervention and no dose-response analysis is presented

The surgical outcomes that most impress, median relapse-free survival not reached and 88.9% post-surgical survival, come from the 8 or 9 patients who were resected, a subgroup defined by having responded

Two patients were offered liver transplantation after their disease remained unresectable but controlled, and both recurred at 16 and 17 months with a single lung lesion each; these two cases are the paper's only transplant data and are frequently cited as if they were a protocol

BTG, which manufactures the microspheres, part-funded the trial, the first author declares BTG grants and fees during its conduct, and one author was a BTG employee at publication, while the confirmatory randomised trial SIRCCA was still enrolling

Low albumin and high carcinoembryonic antigen were the only independent survival predictors, which suggests the outcomes are driven by baseline host and tumour burden rather than by the radioembolisation
The accompanying JAMA Oncology editorial by Scott and Shroff (PMID 31670748) is titled to say the jury is still out; its full text was not read here and only the title is relied on
31670746.n: 41 patients with locally advanced unresectable intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma forming the intention-to-treat population, from 56 screened at 7 French SIRT-experienced centres between November 2013 and June 2016; 32 were analysable per protocol after 9 major protocol deviations, 27 had disease confined to one hemiliver and 12 had cirrhosis
31670746.bottom_line: MISPHEC is the trial behind using yttrium-90 radioembolisation with first-line cisplatin-gemcitabine to downstage locally advanced iCCA, with a 39% response rate, 22% taken to surgery and 20% resected R0, and 22-month median survival. Being single-arm in a favourable locally advanced population at SIRT-experienced centres, it cannot attribute any of that to the radioembolisation. It does establish one hard finding: hepatic failure in 9 of 12 cirrhotic patients, irreversible in 5, so the combination should not be given in cirrhosis.
31670746.funding: Partially funded by BTG Corporation, the microsphere manufacturer, and the Ligue Contre le Cancer, with the funders stated to have had no role in design, conduct, analysis or manuscript approval; the first author declares consultancy, grants and personal fees from BTG during the conduct of the study and one author was employed by BTG at publication

limitations: As with all single-institution phase 2 trials, there is the possibility of selection bias owing to the small sample size
The 10-patient confirmation cohort suggests the therapy can be given elsewhere with comparable safety and efficacy, but a larger number of institutions is needed to validate this
Larger cohorts are necessary to confirm the association between IDH mutations and treatment response
The authors state that a multicentre randomised study of pump-based hepatic arterial infusion is warranted to determine whether liver-directed therapy belongs in first-line treatment
critique: The primary endpoint is 6-month progression-free survival against a single-arm 80% target, so the trial can only show that the regimen beats a number the investigators chose, not that it beats systemic chemotherapy; the 25-month median survival is set against the 11.7 months of ABC-02, a trial with a different and far more advanced population

The cohort is doubly selected: 84 screened, 42 taken to the operating room for pump placement, 38 treated, so the reported outcomes describe patients fit enough for laparotomy with liver-confined disease and no ascites, and the 46 who did not reach treatment are not described in the survival analysis

The 6-month progression-free survival estimate is given with a one-sided 90% confidence interval of 74.8% to infinity, a bound that cannot be used to judge precision and is a consequence of the single-arm design
Only 4 of 38 patients (11%) became resectable, and the resection figures that make the regimen attractive as a conversion strategy rest on those four cases

The IDH1/2 survival signal, 90% against 33% 2-year survival at P = 0.01, comes from 33 sequenced patients with no corresponding progression-free survival difference (14.1 against 10.9 months, P = 0.42), and the authors themselves note it may reflect subsequent resection and off-protocol IDH1-directed therapy rather than sensitivity to this regimen

Dose delivery deteriorated substantially: 71% received the expected floxuridine dose over the first 3 months but only 47% over the next 6, and oxaliplatin was stopped after 8 cycles in 80%, so the regimen that produced these outcomes was not the regimen as written

Hepatobiliary toxicity was common and under-emphasised in the conclusion: grade 3 ALT in 42%, AST in 34% and bilirubin in 18%, with 11% requiring biliary stents including two for chemotherapy-induced biliary sclerosis

Grade 4 pump or arterial complications forced withdrawal in 4 of 38 (11%) at the lead centre and the figure was 30% in the 10-patient confirmatory cohort, which argues against the paper's reading that the confirmatory cohort supports broader applicability

The node-positive comparison, 50% against 60% 2-year survival at P = 0.66, is presented as evidence that nodal disease does not matter, but 18 node-positive patients cannot exclude a clinically important difference
The trial requires an implanted pump programme with both surgical and medical expertise, so nothing in the design tests whether the approach is deliverable outside two academic centres

The accompanying JAMA Oncology editorial by Scott and Shroff (PMID 31670748) was titled to say the jury is still out on locoregional treatment in unresectable cholangiocarcinoma; the editorial's full text was not read here and only its title is relied on
31670750.n: 38 patients with unresectable liver-confined intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma treated at Memorial Sloan Kettering between 2013 and 2019, from 84 screened and 42 who had a hepatic artery infusion pump placed, plus a 10-patient confirmatory cohort at Washington University; median tumour size 8.3 cm, 66% bilobar, 47% with proven nodal disease
31670750.bottom_line: This single-arm phase 2 trial is the strongest prospective evidence for hepatic arterial infusion floxuridine with systemic gemcitabine-oxaliplatin in liver-confined unresectable iCCA: 58% response, 11.8 months median progression-free survival and 25.0 months median overall survival. It cannot show that the pump adds anything, because the comparison is with historical systemic series and only 38 of 84 screened patients were treated. Four patients became resectable, biliary toxicity was frequent, and 11% to 30% had grade 4 pump or arterial complications depending on the centre.
31670750.funding: No sponsor named for the trial itself; funding was obtained by the senior author and the conflict-of-interest statement lists research funding and advisory roles for several investigators with AbbVie, Seattle Genetics, Bayer, Proteus, Roche/Genentech, Boehringer Ingelheim, Eisai and Exelixis among others

limitations: There is no active comparator group
The design precludes any assessment of how much the FGFR alterations themselves contribute to the survival results, since FGFR-altered cholangiocarcinoma may have a more favourable natural history
Including patients with extrahepatic disease could have complicated the analyses, because intrahepatic and extrahepatic tumours have markedly different characteristics

Response duration and progression-free survival were short in some patients despite the presence of a driver alteration, which the authors attribute to clonal evolution and acquired resistance mutations
The 9% prevalence figure for FGFR2 alterations comes from patients centrally prescreened for this trial, not from an unselected population
critique: A single-arm trial cannot measure an effect size, and the comparison that makes the result look decisive, 35.5% against a pooled 9.5% response and 6.9 against 2.6 months progression-free survival with second-line chemotherapy, is drawn from separate literature with different populations
Overall survival of 21.1 months is reported at 40 of 107 deaths with an upper bound of not estimable; at 37% of events a median survival figure is a provisional number being used as a headline

The two negative cohorts carry the trial's real information: 0 of 20 with other FGF/FGFR alterations and 0 of 18 with none responded, which means the FGFR2 fusion cohort is a selected subset and the drug has no activity outside it, so the 1206-patient prescreen is the real denominator

56 distinct fusion partners were observed and 42 occurred in a single patient each, so the biomarker that defines eligibility is a heterogeneous collection and no partner-specific activity can be established from this sample

Progression-free survival at 12 months is only 29% against a 35.5% response rate, so most responses were lost inside a year; the acquired-resistance explanation is offered from the literature rather than from resistance sequencing in this cohort

Hyperphosphataemia affected 60% of patients and 64% had a grade 3 or worse event, with 42% requiring dose interruption and 14% reduction, so the dose that produced these responses is not the dose most patients stayed on

The primary endpoint cohort mixes intrahepatic with extrahepatic, gallbladder and ampullary cases in the overall population of 146 while the responding cohort is 98% intrahepatic, so the anatomical and molecular selections are confounded in the way the paper's own limitation concedes but the conclusion does not reflect

Incyte designed the trial, compiled and analysed the data and paid for the writing, and the trial supported regulatory approval of Incyte's drug on single-arm data with no independent analysis described

The population is second-line or later with no information on earlier use; FIGHT-302, the randomised first-line comparison, was only recruiting at publication, so the drug entered practice before any randomised evidence existed
The publication has since been corrected online, with the corrected version appearing in 2023, and the paper as read does not state what changed
A linked Comment by Yang and colleagues (Lancet Oncology 2020;21:610-612, PMID 32203699) accompanies the article; it was identified from the citation record and not read here
32203698.n: 146 patients with previously treated locally advanced or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma enrolled from 146 sites between 2017 and 2019 into three cohorts by central FGF/FGFR status, 107 with FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements, 20 with other FGF/FGFR alterations and 18 with none; 89% had intrahepatic disease and 1206 patients were centrally prescreened to find the 107
32203698.bottom_line: FIGHT-202 showed that pemigatinib produces centrally confirmed responses in 35.5% of patients with FGFR2-fusion cholangiocarcinoma and none at all in patients without that alteration, which is what made FGFR2 testing mandatory in this disease. It cannot quantify benefit, being single-arm with the comparison made across studies, and the 21.1-month median survival rests on 40 of 107 deaths. Only 9% of 1206 prescreened patients were eligible, across 56 different fusion partners, and 12-month progression-free survival was 29%.
32203698.funding: Incyte Corporation, which designed the study with input from two lead investigators, compiled and analysed the data with the corresponding author, interpreted the data with all authors and funded the medical writing; most authors report Incyte grants or consulting fees

limitations: The overall survival difference was not significant, which the authors attribute partly to placebo-to-ivosidenib crossover and to data being immature at 42% of events at the primary analysis
Limited patient-reported outcome data collection prevented a thorough evaluation of relevant quality-of-life parameters in this population
The authors state there was no justification for withholding ivosidenib from placebo patients at progression, which is why crossover was built in
critique: The primary endpoint is a 1.3-month difference in median progression-free survival, 2.7 against 1.4 months, in a disease assessed by scans at fixed intervals; the hazard ratio of 0.37 is driven by how quickly the placebo arm progressed rather than by how long the treated arm did not

The objective response rate is 3 of 124 (2%), so the drug almost never shrinks tumours and the entire benefit is classified as stable disease, an endpoint that depends on the imaging interval and on no tumour growth being detected

The significant survival figure exists only after rank-preserving structural failure time adjustment, which assumes the treatment effect is the same whenever it is given; the unadjusted intention-to-treat result is HR 0.69 (0.44-1.10), p = 0.060, and the adjusted placebo median of 6.0 months is a modelled quantity, not an observed one
57% of placebo patients crossed over, so the trial was designed in a way that guaranteed its survival endpoint could not be read directly, and that was known at the design stage

Quality-of-life change scores at cycle 2 day 1 were available for 62 of 113 ivosidenib and 20 of 52 placebo patients, so the physical-functioning difference of 9.8 points (2.8-16.7) rests on a third of the placebo arm and is open to differential dropout by disease state
Plasma 2-hydroxyglutarate fell up to 97%, which demonstrates target engagement and not clinical benefit; the paper presents the two together

Only 9 of 185 patients (5%) had cirrhosis and the population is largely metastatic, so the trial describes a non-cirrhotic chemotherapy-refractory population and says nothing about the cirrhotic or liver-confined patients for whom IDH1 status is now also tested

Serious adverse events were 30% against 22% and ascites was the commonest grade 3 event in both arms at 7%, which means the main severe event in the trial is a feature of the disease rather than a drug effect, and the safety comparison is correspondingly uninformative
Agios had a role in design, collection, analysis and interpretation of a trial of its own drug and funded the writing, with no independent statistical oversight described

The result applies only to the roughly 13% of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas with an IDH1 mutation and requires central next-generation sequencing, so the trial's applicability depends on testing infrastructure it does not measure
The publication has been corrected twice, in September 2020 and January 2024, and the version read does not state what was corrected

A linked Comment by de la Fouchardiere (PMID 32416071) and linked correspondence by Gervaso, Pellicori and Fazio with the authors' reply (PMID 32758465 and 32758466) exist; all were identified from the citation record and not read here
32416072.n: 185 patients with advanced IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma that had progressed after chemotherapy, randomised 2:1 at 49 hospitals in six countries between 2017 and 2019 to ivosidenib (124) or placebo (61); 94% had received prior platinum, only 5% had cirrhosis, and IDH1 R132C was the mutation in 70%
32416072.bottom_line: ClarIDHy is the randomised, placebo-controlled trial that established mutant-IDH1 inhibition as a real target in cholangiocarcinoma, with progression-free survival HR 0.37 (0.25-0.54) and a smaller decline in physical functioning. The magnitude is small and the mechanism is stabilisation, not shrinkage: 1.3 months of median progression-free survival and a 2% response rate. Overall survival was not significant as randomised, p = 0.060, and the survival claim depends on a crossover-adjustment model applied to a trial in which 57% of the placebo arm crossed over.
32416072.funding: Agios Pharmaceuticals, which had a role in study design, data collection, data analysis and data interpretation and supplied the medical writing; the first and last authors had full data access and final responsibility for publication

limitations: The trial is not randomised, which the authors call an obvious limitation, defended on the grounds that a randomised trial in a disease this rare is difficult to design
The prescreening population probably already contained patients with known BRAF V600E status because several sites test locally, so the 9% mutation rate is higher than published reports
Central confirmation of histology was not in the protocol, so similar histological subtypes appear under different names in the baseline table according to investigator entry
The study database was not designed to capture previous or subsequent chemotherapy as regimens, only as individual drugs
The published figures are interim results from a trial that remained active
critique: With no control arm, the 51% response rate cannot be turned into a survival benefit, and the comparisons offered in the discussion, ivosidenib 2%, selumetinib 12%, pembrolizumab 6% and FOLFOX median survival of 6 months in ABC-06, are all drawn from other trials with different populations
The headline response rate is investigator-assessed at 51% while independent central review gave 47% with no complete responses, and the paper leads with the investigator figure

Durability collapses with time: responses were ongoing in 36% at 12 months and 13% at 24 months, and progression-free survival fell from 63% at 6 months to 8% at 24, so the 9-month median duration of response is the generous reading of a short-lived effect

Patients with bilirubin above three times normal or untreatable biliary obstruction were excluded, which removes much of real advanced biliary practice and selects for preserved liver function, making the survival figures optimistic for the clinic
Dose reduction was needed in 35% and interruption in 56%, with a median exposure of 8 months, so the regimen as delivered differs substantially from 150 mg twice daily plus 2 mg daily

All 16 sequenced tumours had tumour mutational burden below 6 mutations per Mb and the biomarker analyses involved 16 to 19 patients, so the translational component cannot support or refute anything and is reported as if informative

Two patients (5%) died of sepsis judged unrelated to treatment while on a combination whose commonest treatment-related serious event was pyrexia in 19%; the attribution of those deaths is investigator-determined with no independent adjudication described

The trial changed sponsor mid-conduct from GlaxoSmithKline to Novartis, with data collection and analysis transferring between two companies and Novartis employees as authors, and no independent analysis is described
The trial is a basket cohort of 43 patients reported as a standalone result, so the multiplicity across the basket's other cohorts is not accounted for in the confidence interval presented

One patient who responded went on to cholecystectomy, hepatectomy and lymphadenectomy; a single case is reported in a way that invites reading the regimen as a conversion strategy, which 43 patients cannot support
Linked correspondence by van Golen and Dekker with the authors' reply (Lancet Oncol 2020;21:e515, PMID 33152306 and 33152307) exists; it was identified from the citation record and not read here
32818466.n: 43 patients with BRAF V600E-mutated biliary tract cancer previously treated with gemcitabine-based chemotherapy, enrolled at 19 sites in nine countries between March 2014 and July 2018 from 626 locally prescreened patients in whom 57 BRAF V600E mutations were found; 39 of 43 (91%) had intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and the mutation was centrally confirmed in 39 of 43
32818466.bottom_line: ROAR showed that dabrafenib plus trametinib produces responses in roughly half of patients with BRAF V600E biliary tract cancer, a cohort that is 91% intrahepatic, with median progression-free survival of 9 months. It is a single-arm interim analysis with no comparator, an investigator-assessed primary endpoint that central review scored lower, and only 8% of patients progression-free at 24 months. BRAF V600E was found in 9% here only because sites entered patients already known to carry it; in practice the yield is lower, and jaundiced patients were excluded.
32818466.funding: GlaxoSmithKline, which originally designed and sponsored the trial and initially performed data collection and analysis, with Novartis Pharmaceuticals as current sponsor and funder of the medical writing; Novartis employees are among the authors

limitations: The trial was conducted in a single country, and UK first-line practice of stopping chemotherapy at 6 months differs from countries that treat to progression, with unknown effect on second-line efficacy
Countries had varying access to molecular profiling, especially during recruitment
There was insufficient power for subgroup analyses, which the authors acknowledge challenges some interpretations in such a heterogeneous disease
Routine radiological follow-up was not performed in the active symptom control group, so progression-free survival and response data exist only for the chemotherapy arm
Three-monthly imaging, no central radiology review and the open-label design might have affected the progression-free survival results
Subsequent lines of treatment were given at clinician discretion and could have affected overall survival, although the authors state the proportions were balanced
Stratification errors from incorrect baseline data supplied at randomisation were discovered during data cleaning and required a post hoc sensitivity analysis
Quality-of-life and health-economic analyses were not reported with the primary results
critique: The absolute difference in median overall survival is 0.9 months, 6.2 against 5.3, against grade 3 to 5 adverse events in 69% of the chemotherapy arm and three chemotherapy-related deaths from infection, acute kidney injury and febrile neutropenia

The adjusted hazard ratio of 0.69 (0.50-0.97) at p = 0.031 just clears conventional significance in a trial powered for HR 0.63 on 148 deaths, and the sensitivity analysis required after the stratification errors gives 0.68 (0.49-0.95), so the result sits close to the boundary under either model

Platinum sensitivity was itself independently prognostic, adjusted HR 0.71 (0.49-1.00), and was imbalanced against the chemotherapy arm, 67% platinum resistant or refractory against 58% in the control arm; the minimisation variable that mattered most was the one that failed

Objective response was 4 of 81 (5%) and 37% of the chemotherapy arm had progressive disease on first assessment, so for most patients FOLFOX did nothing measurable to the tumour while producing the toxicity recorded

6 of 81 assigned FOLFOX never received it and 9 received only one cycle, while 8 of 81 in the control arm received off-study chemotherapy, so roughly a fifth of the randomised contrast was diluted in both directions

Progression-free survival and radiological response can only be reported for one arm because the control arm had no scheduled imaging, which means the trial has no comparative disease-control data at all and the survival difference cannot be attributed to any observed antitumour effect
The three chemotherapy-related deaths amount to 3.7% of the FOLFOX arm, a mortality figure of the same order as the median survival gain, and the paper does not set the two against each other
