Baseline albumin of 35 g/L or above carried an adjusted HR of 0.54 (0.37-0.78), a larger prognostic effect than the treatment itself, which indicates the population is dominated by performance and nutritional state rather than by second-line chemotherapy

44% of patients had intrahepatic disease and no site-specific hazard ratio is reported, with the authors conceding subgroup power was insufficient, so an iCCA-specific second-line benefit is not demonstrated

The trial's comparator and context are now historical: with first-line immunotherapy and FGFR2 or IDH1 inhibitors available for roughly a third of intrahepatic patients, who would be offered FOLFOX in the second line has changed, and no molecular profiling was performed here

Four linked correspondence letters with an authors' reply appeared in Lancet Oncology 2021;22(7):e284-e289 (PMIDs 34197747, 34197748, 34197749, 34197750, reply 34197751); their content was not available here, so none of their arguments is represented
33798493.n: 162 patients with advanced biliary tract cancer progressing after first-line cisplatin-gemcitabine, randomised 1:1 at 20 UK centres from 290 screened between 27 March 2014 and 4 January 2018; 72 of 162 (44%) had intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and 133 (82%) were metastatic
33798493.bottom_line: ABC-06 is the only randomised evidence for second-line chemotherapy in advanced biliary tract cancer, and it is positive: adjusted HR 0.69 (0.50-0.97), with 12-month survival of 25.9% against 11.4%. The absolute median gain is 0.9 months, bought with 69% grade 3 to 5 toxicity and three treatment-related deaths, and the response rate was 5%. Stratification errors required a post hoc sensitivity analysis, the control arm had no imaging so there is no comparative disease-control data, and 44% intrahepatic disease was never analysed separately.
33798493.funding: Cancer Research UK, StandUpToCancer, AMMF (The UK Cholangiocarcinoma Charity) and The Christie Charity, with additional funding from The Cholangiocarcinoma Foundation and a Conquer Cancer Foundation Young Investigator Award; the funders peer-reviewed for patient acceptability but had no role in design, and The Christie NHS Foundation Trust sponsored it as an investigator-initiated study

limitations: All 20 included studies were retrospective, so selection bias exists in how patients were chosen for thermal ablation, although the authors argue a prospective study is hard to mount in a disease that is only 10% of primary liver cancer
Discordant reporting of results, including survival outcomes, limited the ability to generate combined estimates
Heterogeneity was present across the selection criteria for ablation and across the patient populations

Technical aspects, CT versus ultrasound guidance, single versus multiple probes, and general anaesthesia versus sedation, could not be analysed because of insufficient detail and too few studies, and could be confounders
A lack of individual patient-level data limited the meta-regression
The authors report their own evidence of publication bias on the 3-year overall survival pooling, Egger P = 0.039
A randomised study is required to determine any difference in efficacy between radiofrequency and microwave ablation
critique: Pooled survival of 42.1% at 3 years and 28.5% at 5 years is reported with heterogeneity of I squared 68% to 85%; at that level a single pooled proportion describes no real population, and the random-effects interval quoted is a confidence interval for an average, not a prediction interval for the next patient

Parity with resection is asserted by setting 28.5% pooled 5-year survival against the 30% from the Mavros resection meta-analysis, two different literatures with different stage distributions, eras and candidacy, compared without any adjustment and across non-overlapping confidence bounds that are never computed

The 3 cm recommendation that the paper exists to deliver rests on a dichotomised study-level hazard ratio, 2.12 (1.24-3.63), from aggregate data; the threshold was not derived, it was the cut-point the included studies happened to report

The three prognostic hazard ratios for size, number and age are univariable study-level estimates that could not be adjusted for one another, nor for nodal status, margin, liver function or performance status, so they cannot be used as a selection rule in combination, which is how they are used

The patients behind these estimates were chosen for ablation because their tumours were small and accessible or because they were medically inoperable; the pooled survival therefore mixes a favourable tumour selection with an unfavourable patient selection and the two cannot be separated from aggregate data

Recurrence-free survival of 40.0% at 1 year and 19.2% at 3 years, the numbers that most limit the treatment, could be pooled from only 4 of 20 studies, and freedom from local tumour progression from 5; the headline overall survival therefore comes from a much larger and differently selected evidence base than the disease control figures

Technical efficacy of 91.9% pools individual study rates ranging from 66.7% to 100%, so a third of patients failed complete ablation in the worst-reporting study, and the technique that produced the pooled figure cannot be identified because no technical variable could be analysed
Included studies were 10 to 107 patients each, so a handful of larger series dominate the random-effects weights, and no leave-one-out or influence analysis is reported

The literature is heavily weighted to Chinese and Korean series and restricted to English-language publications, which is both a geographical and a language restriction on a pooled estimate presented as general

Newcastle-Ottawa scores of 6 to 8 are reported but no study was excluded on quality and no sensitivity analysis by quality score is presented, so study quality enters the pooling only as a description
Ablation generates no nodal information and the review does not address nodal staging at all, although node status is the variable that most changes management in this disease

Overall survival was pooled as proportions at fixed time points rather than from reconstructed time-to-event data, so no median survival, no numbers at risk and no hazard comparison against any alternative treatment can be read from the analysis
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed, so the only critical reading available is the authors' own
34347159.n: 917 patients with mass-forming intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma treated by radiofrequency or microwave ablation, pooled from 20 retrospective observational studies published up to 11 March 2021, of whom 502 had primary tumours, 355 post-resection recurrence and 60 were unspecified
34347159.bottom_line: Pooling 917 ablated patients across 20 retrospective series gives the field its working numbers: 82.4% survival at 1 year falling to 28.5% at 5, 91.9% technical success, 5.7% major complications, and worse survival above 3 cm, with multiple tumours or over 65. It does not show that ablation matches resection, because the 30% surgical figure it is compared with comes from a separate meta-analysis of a differently selected population, and the pooled estimates carry I squared up to 85% with Egger evidence of publication bias at 3 years. Only four of the twenty studies contributed recurrence-free survival, which at 40% at one year is the number that bounds the treatment.
34347159.funding: The authors state that the work received no funding and declare no relationships with any company whose products or services relate to the subject matter

limitations: The treatment effect estimate on the primary overall survival analysis was very likely confounded by the allowance of crossover, which was built in on the advice of patient advocacy groups and clinicians to support accrual in a rare biomarker-selected population
Quality-of-life analyses were limited by small sample sizes at day 1 of cycle 2 and cycle 3, partly because of rapid progression and withdrawal
The comutation analysis was limited by the absence of on-study biopsies, so resistance mechanisms are unknown and are being pursued in separate circulating tumour DNA studies
critique: The final intention-to-treat overall survival result is negative, HR 0.79 (0.56-1.12), one-sided P = .09 on 150 events, and the positive claim comes entirely from a rank-preserving structural failure time model that assumes the drug's effect is identical whenever it is given

The model-derived placebo median of 5.1 months is 2.4 months shorter than the 7.5 months actually observed, so the adjusted comparison replaces measured survival in the control arm with an estimate generated under the assumption being tested

70% of placebo patients, 43 of 61, crossed over; a design that routes the majority of controls onto the experimental drug cannot answer a survival question, and the paper describes this trade-off as supporting accrual rather than as removing the endpoint

Objective response was 2%, three partial responses, and the clinical signal is 51% against 28% stable disease, a category whose size depends on the scan interval; median treatment duration was 2.8 against 1.6 months

The comparator is placebo rather than the second-line standard established by ABC-06, so the trial establishes activity against nothing and not benefit against what a patient would otherwise be offered

Quality-of-life differences of 11.0 and 12.3 points are reported with P values from timepoints where, in the companion primary publication, fewer than half the placebo patients contributed data; the patients who felt worst progressed and left the study, which biases a between-arm comparison of those who remained

Baseline ascites was present in 27% and 21% of the arms, so the commonest grade 3 or worse event, ascites in 9% against 7%, is largely a disease event and the safety comparison carries almost no information about the drug

Protocol deviations are visible in the baseline data, with one ivosidenib patient at ECOG performance status 3 and one placebo patient at 2 against a stated requirement of 0 to 1, and these are not addressed in the analysis

The 10.3-month median survival is said to compare favourably with the published literature on chemotherapy and other targeted agents, a cross-trial comparison made in place of the randomised comparison the trial could not deliver
Only 15% of patients remained on ivosidenib for a year, so the benefit as experienced by most patients is a few weeks of radiographic stability
Agios designed the trial and analysed the data for its own drug, with company employees and stockholders as authors and no independent statistical replication described
The paper describes its own findings as heralding a paradigm shift in the same paragraph that concedes the primary survival analysis was confounded

Linked commentary and correspondence on the ClarIDHy primary report (de la Fouchardiere, PMID 32416071; Gervaso, Pellicori and Fazio, PMID 32758465) were paywalled and not read; the cost-effectiveness point attributed to them is second-hand and should be treated as provisional
34554208.n: 187 patients with unresectable or metastatic IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma randomised 2:1 at 49 hospitals in six countries between February 2017 and May 2020, 126 ivosidenib and 61 placebo; 171 of 187 (over 90%) had intrahepatic disease, 93% were metastatic, 47% had had two prior lines and 70% carried IDH1 R132C
34554208.bottom_line: This is the final overall survival report of ClarIDHy and the reason ivosidenib is used in IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma: median survival 10.3 against 7.5 months with preserved physical functioning and a tolerable safety profile. The survival endpoint was not met as randomised, HR 0.79 (0.56-1.12), P = .09, and the significant figure requires a crossover-adjustment model in a trial where 70% of controls crossed over. Response was 2%, so nothing here suggests the drug can convert unresectable disease.
34554208.funding: Agios Pharmaceuticals, which designed the study and analysed the data and funded the medical writing; several authors were Agios employees or stockholders and the academic authors declare extensive consultancies and research funding across the industry

limitations: No limitations section; the authors concede within the text that retrospective comparisons of liver resection against transplantation are subject to selection bias and to both unmeasured and residual confounding, given how distinct the two populations are
They state that a fair comparison between resection and transplantation is unlikely to be possible in any retrospective design, and that a randomised comparison is not feasible

They list the National Cancer Database analysis's own gaps, including no fibrosis or cirrhosis score, no MELD score, no functional status, no detail on neoadjuvant cycles, no future liver remnant, no tumour number and no operative detail

They note that the 61.4% neoadjuvant chemotherapy and 42.1% neoadjuvant radiation rates in the transplant arm of that database raise the possibility that some perihilar cholangiocarcinoma or HCC was miscoded as intrahepatic
They state that pooling intrahepatic with perihilar disease, and patients who did and did not receive neoadjuvant or adjuvant therapy, is a significant limitation on interpreting the data
They concede that a resectable iCCA should be resected given organ scarcity, and that waitlist outcomes for iCCA and HCC cannot be compared
critique: A narrative invited review with no stated search strategy, no inclusion criteria for the series it tabulates and no pooling; the tabulated experience spans 1988 to 2020 across changing imaging, pathology definitions and chemotherapy, and the reader cannot tell which series were considered and left out

Almost all the transplant experience quoted is of iCCA found incidentally or misdiagnosed as HCC, so the survival figures describe populations defined after the operation; dropout before transplantation is absent from every series cited and the review does not quantify it

Several of the cited series pool pure iCCA with mixed HCC-CCA, which can make survival look favourable when the dominant phenotype is HCC; the review notes this but still carries those survival numbers into its summary tables

The De Martin comparison that most favours transplantation, 75% versus 36% 5-year recurrence-free survival with HR 0.23 (0.07-0.82), has a confidence interval reaching 0.82 and comes from a retrospective multicentre series with no matching described in the review

The National Cancer Database propensity-matched comparison the review also cites found 38.8% versus 34.9% 5-year survival, a difference of under four points in 57 pairs, and the review calls this equipoise rather than a null result

The 2020 meta-analysis figure for single iCCA 2 cm or less, 67% 5-year recurrence-free survival, has a confidence interval of 47-86 and is pooled across studies with different size and histology definitions, so it carries the same heterogeneity the review criticises elsewhere

The six-month stability requirement the review promotes into its treatment algorithm comes from Lunsford's six transplanted patients with a median cumulative tumour diameter of 14.2 cm; the review applies it to patients without cirrhosis as a general principle on that evidence

The conditional recommendation for upfront transplantation at 2 cm or less rests on the authors' own 15-patient explant series, and the senior author is an author of that series, so the review's central recommendation is self-citing

The three prospective trials tabulated (NCT02878473, TESLA NCT04556214, and the Toronto living-donor protocol) had enrolled only a handful of patients between them at the time of writing, which the table does not state, so the pipeline looks more mature than it was

The senior author discloses consultancy for AstraZeneca, Roche and Novartis and grant support from Bayer and Roche while the review discusses systemic therapy as the gateway to transplantation; two of the three authors have no disclosure recorded at all

The review was overtaken quickly: TOPAZ-1 is described as ongoing, and the EASL-ILCA guideline with its 3 cm transplant threshold appeared the following year, so the thresholds the review states as current were superseded
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed for this review, so the only critical reading available is internal to the text
34859465.bottom_line: A useful tabulation of every published transplant series for iCCA up to 2020, which establishes that outcomes in single tumours of 2 cm or less look better than in larger or multifocal disease and that no comparison with resection is free of selection bias. It does not establish a threshold, a stability requirement or an indication, because every number it reports comes from cohorts defined by explant pathology with no measure of waitlist dropout. Its central recommendations cite the senior author's own 15-patient series and a six-patient case series.
34859465.funding: No funding statement beyond a declaration that the work had not been submitted elsewhere; Sapisochin discloses consultancy for AstraZeneca, Roche and Novartis and grant support from Bayer and Roche, and no disclosure is recorded for the other two authors

limitations: The authors concede that the 2 cm T-stage cut-off in the LCSGJ staging system needs further validation
They state there is little evidence on the weight that should be given to major biliary invasion in staging
The significance of lymph node dissection is stated to be currently unclear, with no recommendation made
They state there is no high-quality evidence for selecting which patients should receive adjuvant chemotherapy
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is recorded as having no evidence of benefit, with no recommendation made
The literature search closed at the end of 2019
critique: The guideline is framed for Japanese national health insurance, so reimbursement enters the recommendations as if it were evidence: ivosidenib is dismissed as uninsured and adjuvant capecitabine is downgraded in part because it is not reimbursed in Japan rather than on trial data

The first-line recommendation of gemcitabine-cisplatin-S-1 rests on a single Japan-only phase 3 with a 0.9-month median survival gain and a 90% confidence interval of 0.628 to 0.996 that nearly touches 1, and S-1 is unavailable in North America and Europe, so the top recommendation cannot be acted on outside Asia
A 90% rather than 95% confidence interval is quoted for the pivotal first-line hazard ratio without comment, which is a lower evidential bar than the rest of the document's recommendations imply

Hepatectomy for a solitary node-negative tumour is recommended with no restriction on tumour size, while the guideline's own staging system uses 2 cm as a T-stage boundary and its own survival data show 63.4% 5-year survival below 2 cm; the recommendation and the staging contradict each other on whether size matters
No recommendation is made on lymph node dissection, so a guideline that conditions its entire treatment algorithm on nodal metastasis gives no guidance on how nodal status is to be established

The staging system used is incompatible with the UICC 8th edition used elsewhere, with a 2 cm rather than 5 cm T cut-off and major biliary invasion retained after UICC dropped periductal invasion, so survival figures and stage groupings in this guideline cannot be compared with international series

Survival figures by tumour number, 46.8%, 33.6% and 11.1% for one, two and three tumours, are presented as decision thresholds with no cohort, period or source denominators given in the recommendation text

Conversion-to-resection rates of 36.4% to 53% after chemotherapy are quoted alongside a no-recommendation verdict on neoadjuvant therapy, and the claim that converted patients survive 24.1 months against 25.7 for primarily resectable patients is a comparison of two non-randomised groups presented as reassurance

Percutaneous ablation is placed last, only when both resection and drug therapy are precluded, while stereotactic radiotherapy for tumours up to 5 cm and particle radiotherapy with no size limit are both weakly recommended; the relative ordering of the local therapies is not justified by any comparative data

Transplantation is dismissed as generally not indicated with no size-stratified discussion, which puts this guideline directly at odds with the EASL-ILCA and ILTS-ILCA positions on cirrhotic tumours of 2 to 3 cm

Biopsy is recommended only in unresectable cases, which means resection decisions are made on imaging alone and the small-duct against large-duct subtyping the guideline describes cannot be used preoperatively
Several authors hold senior editorial positions at the journal that published the guideline, including its editor-in-chief, which is disclosed but not addressed
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed, so no independent published appraisal accompanies the first Japanese iCCA guideline
35978598.bottom_line: The first Japanese iCCA guideline, and the clearest statement of a hepatic-reserve-driven algorithm: resect a solitary node-negative tumour at any size, treat nodal or multifocal disease with drugs first, and give gemcitabine-cisplatin-S-1 for unresectable disease. It is built on the LCSGJ staging system with a 2 cm T cut-off, which is incompatible with the UICC 8th edition used elsewhere, and its first-line regimen rests on a Japan-only trial with a 0.9-month gain and a drug unavailable in the West. It makes no recommendation on lymph node dissection while conditioning its whole algorithm on nodal status.
35978598.funding: The authors state they have no funding source and no conflicts of interest to declare; several authors hold editorial positions at the publishing journal, including the editor-in-chief, three associate editors and one editorial board member of Liver Cancer

limitations: The document states that too few randomised trials exist for a GRADE-based guideline, so all 53 statements are expert panel consensus with no formal rating of evidence quality or strength of recommendation
Surveillance is explicitly not recommended in patients under 18 or with small-duct primary sclerosing cholangitis, an acknowledged gap rather than a positive recommendation
Elevated CA 19-9 alone is stated to be insufficient to diagnose cholangiocarcinoma
The panel states that locoregional therapy for iCCA is not yet standard and that transplantation for unresectable liver-limited iCCA belongs only in research protocols
critique: No prospective study supports annual cholangiocarcinoma surveillance in primary sclerosing cholangitis; the 68% against 20% 5-year survival figure comes from a single retrospective cohort comparison, where the surveyed group is by construction composed of patients well enough to attend surveillance

The guidance contradicts itself on iCCA transplantation: statement 40 confines it to research protocols while the Figure 9A algorithm directs referral to a transplant centre for any unresectable iCCA of 2 cm or less, and a reader following the figure and a reader following the statement will do different things

Two different size thresholds sit in the same document, 2 cm in the iCCA algorithm and 3 cm radial diameter for perihilar transplantation after neoadjuvant therapy, with no explanation of why the intrahepatic limit is tighter

Routine FISH on biliary brushings is recommended for every suspected perihilar or distal cholangiocarcinoma, a test not uniformly available for this purpose even in major centres, and the 70% against 18% figure for serial polysomy is a diagnostic yield over time rather than a test characteristic at the point of decision

Statement 44 forbids fine-needle aspiration or percutaneous biopsy of a perihilar mass to protect transplant candidacy, while statement 34 of the companion literature and most oncology guidance require tissue before systemic therapy; the guidance does not say what to do for a patient who turns out not to be a transplant candidate after the opportunity to biopsy has passed

No statement addresses the role or extent of lymphadenectomy in iCCA, nor a minimum node count in perihilar or distal disease, leaving the operative decision that determines stage unaddressed across 53 statements

Thresholds conflict with European guidance without the conflict being noted: cholecystectomy at a gallbladder polyp above 8 mm against above 6 mm in the 2017 European guidelines, and ursodeoxycholic acid at 13 to 23 mg/kg/day against 15 to 20 mg/kg/day in EASL guidance
Adjuvant capecitabine is recommended for all cholangiocarcinoma without reference to the failed intention-to-treat analysis of the trial behind it or to the absence of an intrahepatic subgroup effect

The diagnostic performance figures are quoted without the cohorts behind them: MRI/MRCP at 89% sensitivity and 75% specificity against ultrasound at 57% and 94%, and CA 19-9 at 129 U/mL giving 78% and 98%, are presented side by side from different studies with different reference standards

PET is recommended against for the primary tumour here while the EASL-ILCA guideline recommends routine FDG-PET for nodal staging in apparently resectable iCCA, a direct conflict between two 2023 guidance documents that neither acknowledges

The guidance introduces new stricture terminology (dominant, high-grade and relevant) whose thresholds are set by expert consensus with no validation data, and then conditions several management statements on those definitions

The transplant author declares consulting and grant relationships with Roche and AstraZeneca and is also the senior author of the iCCA transplant series and review on which the transplant statements depend

An editorial by Saffioti and Mavroeidis (Hepatobiliary Surg Nutr 2024;13:172-5, PMID 38322224) raises the FISH availability and lymphadenectomy gaps; it was identified from the citation record and its arguments are reported second-hand rather than read here
36083140.bottom_line: The AASLD guidance is the reference for surveillance and diagnosis in primary sclerosing cholangitis and the first AASLD document to cover cholangiocarcinoma, with 53 statements spanning annual MRI/MRCP surveillance, intraductal cytology with FISH, mandatory histology for iCCA, and transplantation after neoadjuvant therapy for perihilar tumours of 3 cm or less. It is explicitly expert consensus with no graded evidence, and no prospective study supports its central surveillance recommendation. It contradicts itself on iCCA transplantation, with statement 40 confining it to research protocols and the algorithm figure referring every unresectable tumour of 2 cm or less.
36083140.funding: Funding for the development of the Practice Guidance was provided by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases; individual authors declare grants and advisory relationships including Gilead, Bristol-Myers Squibb, GlaxoSmithKline, Mirum, Boston Scientific, Intercept, Novartis and others, and the transplant author declares consulting and grants from Roche, AstraZeneca and Integra

limitations: No limitations section; the guideline records its uncertainty through evidence grades, with most surgical recommendations at level III to V, that is non-randomised or expert-opinion evidence
Ampullary cancer and mixed hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma are explicitly stated to be outside the scope

External beam radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy as definitive treatment of locally advanced disease is graded II, D, that is recommended against outside trials, and liver transplantation for perihilar disease III, D
Several liver-directed recommendations are graded C, meaning insufficient evidence for efficacy or benefit not outweighing risk, including stereotactic radiotherapy and intra-arterial therapy
critique: The guideline makes no recommendation at all on liver transplantation for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma; transplantation appears only as a III, D statement about perihilar disease, so the question a transplant surgeon is asked most often is simply absent

Adjuvant capecitabine is recommended at II, A on BILCAP's per-protocol median of 53 against 36 months and the adjusted per-protocol hazard ratio of 0.75 (0.58-0.97); the intention-to-treat result that the trial actually prespecified, HR 0.81 (0.63-1.04), p = 0.097, is not quoted beside it

Four anatomically and biologically distinct diseases are managed under one algorithm, with no stratification by subsite for most recommendations and none by aetiology such as liver fluke, hepatolithiasis, primary sclerosing cholangitis or viral hepatitis

Core biopsy before any non-surgical treatment is recommended at III, A with no guidance on what to do when the biopsy is inconclusive, which in this disease is common, and no acknowledgement that biopsy is constrained in prospective transplant candidates by seeding concerns
Surgical technique is not addressed anywhere: there is no recommendation on minimally invasive against open resection despite rapidly growing laparoscopic and robotic practice

The IV, C recommendation to resect laparoscopic port sites at gallbladder cancer re-resection conflicts with published data showing port-site metastases mark peritoneal disease without resection improving survival or recurrence, and the guideline does not engage that evidence

Hepatic arterial infusion is graded III, C although the phase II data it cites report 39% to 56% response rates against roughly 21% with gemcitabine-cisplatin in the ABC trials, so the grade reflects trial design rather than the effect size the guideline itself reports

Durvalumab is recommended at I, A with an ESMO-MCBS score of 4 on a TOPAZ-1 hazard ratio of 0.76, while the absolute median survival gain in that trial was 1.3 months at an interim analysis with proportional hazards violated; the magnitude-of-benefit score is not reconciled with the absolute difference

FGFR inhibitors, pembrolizumab for MSI-high disease and dabrafenib-trametinib are all graded III, A, that is strong recommendations on single-arm evidence, and their response rates of 20-40%, 40.9% and 51% come from trials with no comparator

Routine hepatoduodenal lymphadenectomy for iCCA is recommended at IV, A, a strong recommendation on the weakest evidence level, with no stated number of nodes, no survival estimate and no acknowledgement that the adjuvant trials on which the guideline relies did not mandate it

The lead author declares relationships with more than twenty companies including the manufacturers of durvalumab, pemigatinib, ivosidenib and the microsphere and infusion products discussed, while ESMO reports no external funding for the guideline itself

The guideline was approved for publication in October 2022 and so predates the full ASCOT publication and the HER2 and FGFR approvals that followed, while remaining the parent document for the 2025 interim update
A surgical-oncology commentary by Maker (Hepatobiliary Surg Nutr 2024;13:516-519, PMID 38911219) discusses these guidelines; it was identified from the citation record and not read here
36372281.bottom_line: The ESMO guideline is the reference document for systemic management of biliary tract cancer, and it sets the positions clinicians quote: core biopsy and molecular profiling, resection with lymphadenectomy as the only curative option, adjuvant capecitabine, gemcitabine-cisplatin with durvalumab first line, FOLFOX second line, and graded targeted options by alteration. For iCCA surgery it offers very little: most surgical recommendations are level III to V, technique is not addressed, and transplantation for iCCA is not mentioned at all. Its adjuvant recommendation is built on BILCAP's per-protocol rather than intention-to-treat result.
36372281.funding: No external funding; production costs covered by ESMO central funds, with editorial and ESMO-MCBS support funded by ESMO; the lead author declares speaker, consultancy and advisory fees from more than twenty companies including AstraZeneca, BTG, Incyte, Roche, Servier, Sirtex, Taiho and Terumo, and research funding from Incyte and Servier

limitations: Single-group design and relatively small sample size
The lack of a comparator group precluded accurate quantification of the treatment effect, because estimates of the natural history of FGFR fusion-positive disease are variable
The effect of FGFR inhibition on overall survival is still under investigation in three randomised first-line trials, which were enrolling slowly at the time of writing
Conditional regulatory and reimbursement approval was granted on the basis of single-group data because the cancer is uncommon
All biomarker and subgroup analyses were exploratory
critique: No comparator means the 42% response rate cannot be converted into a benefit estimate, and the comparisons the paper offers, 35.5% for pemigatinib and 23.1% for infigratinib, are cross-trial with different eligibility and different central review processes

Median overall survival of 21.7 months has an upper bound of not reached at a median follow-up of 17.1 months, so the figure most often quoted from this trial is estimated from a follow-up shorter than the median it reports

Only 6 of 43 responders (14%) responded for 12 months or more, while 72% responded for at least 6 months; the durability claim therefore rests on a 6-month landmark, and the 12-month picture is much weaker than the headline suggests

Hyperphosphataemia affected 85% of patients with grade 3 in 30%, and dose interruptions occurred in 50% and reductions in 54%, so more than half of patients were not taking 20 mg daily; the response rate is attributed to a dose most patients did not maintain

The CDKN2A and CDKN2B progression-free survival differences, 4.9 against 9.7 and 4.8 against 11.0 months, are exploratory subgroup comparisons with unadjusted intervals, yet they are the paper's main prognostic claim

783 patients were screened for 103 enrolled, and the paper notes tissue profiling failure in biliary cancer reaching 26.8%, so eligibility depends on an assay pipeline whose performance determines whether the result is reachable at all

Circulating tumour DNA detected the alteration in 83 of 95 tested (87%), which is presented as supporting ctDNA profiling although 12 of 95 known-positive patients were missed, a 13% false-negative rate in patients already known to carry the fusion

36652354.n: 103 patients with unresectable or metastatic FGFR2 fusion-positive or rearrangement-positive intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, enrolled from 783 screened at 47 sites in 13 countries between April 2018 and November 2019, all previously treated with at least one systemic line including gemcitabine-platinum and 53% with two or more prior lines
36652354.bottom_line: FOENIX-CCA2 established futibatinib as active in FGFR2-rearranged intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, with a centrally reviewed response rate of 42%, median progression-free survival of 9.0 months and tolerable toxicity dominated by manageable hyperphosphataemia. 36652354.funding: Taiho Oncology and Taiho Pharmaceutical, which designed the study, with sponsor employees as co-authors, sponsor-funded medical writing and editorial assistance, and author confidentiality agreements; one author was part-funded by the NIHR UCLH-UCL Biomedical Research Centre

limitations: The trial was conducted only in Japanese patients, and S-1 pharmacokinetics and toxicity, particularly diarrhoea, are suggested to differ in European and North American patients, requiring dose adjustment
Statistical power for relapse-free survival was low because of the small number of events, and the Kaplan-Meier curves crossed at 6 years
3-year overall survival in the observation group was 67.6% against a hypothesised 47%, a hypothesis based on outcomes more than ten years earlier

The trial is open-label, which the authors defend as ethically acceptable
Relapse data beyond 3 years should be considered immature with many censored cases
critique: The primary analysis was conducted at 179 deaths, 62.8% of the 285 prespecified events, with a one-sided alpha of 0.05 and the result reported as definitive; the planned 5-year analysis can therefore only weaken, not strengthen, the registration claim

Median overall survival is not estimable in the S-1 arm, with a lower confidence bound of 5.2 years, so the headline rests entirely on a 3-year landmark difference of 9.5 percentage points rather than on any median

Relapse-free survival did not reach significance, HR 0.80 (0.61-1.04), p = 0.088, and the curves cross at 6 years, so the mechanism by which a drug given for 24 weeks improves survival without delaying relapse is not accounted for

Only 13% of patients had intrahepatic disease, and that subgroup's overall survival hazard ratio is 0.75 with an interval of 0.30-1.89 in 58 patients, which is compatible with substantial harm; the Japanese staging system classifies iCCA as primary liver cancer, which is why the stratum is this small

Ampullary carcinoma, excluded from BILCAP as a different disease, is included here and carries the most favourable subgroup hazard ratio of 0.49, so the most responsive tumour type in the trial is the one other trials deliberately left out

Subgroup hazard ratios are quoted for sex (0.51 in women), nodal status, stage and margin, with the R1 subgroup at 1.04 (0.57-1.92); no interaction reached significance, so these differences are being read off a forest plot with no multiplicity control

The control arm is observation, which was already superseded outside Asia by adjuvant capecitabine after BILCAP, so the trial cannot tell a surgeon whether to use S-1 or capecitabine and the two have never been compared

The population was highly selected, 87% performance status 0 and 86% R0, and the control arm did 20 percentage points better than assumed; a trial in that population needs a much larger sample to measure an adjuvant effect reliably
Toxicity was monitored in 207 treated patients while the observation arm received no scheduled treatment contact, so the modest toxicity profile is not a between-arm comparison

An eligible-patients-only analysis (n = 429) is reported alongside intention to treat with hazard ratios of 0.70 and 0.78, a second analysis set presented without stating which was prespecified as supportive

Two published commentaries exist, Chiang and Chen in the Lancet (PMID 36681404) and Sood and Mayo on the eligibility criteria in Annals of Surgical Oncology (PMID 37684366); both were identified from the citation record and not read here
36681415.n: 440 patients randomised at 38 Japanese hospitals between 9 September 2013 and 22 June 2018 after R0 or R1 resection of biliary tract cancer, 222 observation and 218 S-1; only 58 of 440 (13%) had intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and 186 (42%) underwent hepatectomy
36681415.bottom_line: ASCOT is the first adjuvant trial in biliary tract cancer to show a survival benefit on its intention-to-treat primary endpoint, 3-year survival 77.1% against 67.6% with S-1, HR 0.69 (0.51-0.94). It does not establish adjuvant therapy for resected iCCA: 13% of patients had intrahepatic disease with a subgroup interval of 0.30 to 1.89, relapse-free survival was not significant and its curves cross, and the analysis was done at 63% of the planned events. S-1 is also not an option outside Asia, and it has never been compared with capecitabine.
36681415.funding: The National Cancer Center Research and Development Fund and the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare of Japan; the funders had no role in design, collection, analysis, interpretation or writing, but individual authors declare extensive industry grants and honoraria including from Delta-Fly Pharma, Eisai, Yakult, AstraZeneca, Ono and many others

limitations: Participants with intrahepatic tumours were enrolled disproportionately relative to population frequencies, leaving smaller samples for extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer and affecting those subgroup analyses
The requirement for tumour tissue at entry may have contributed to a selection bias towards intrahepatic tumours because they are more accessible for sampling
Outcomes could not be assessed by microsatellite instability status because only ten participants with known MSI-high tumours were enrolled
Translational biomarker analyses are still ongoing and a dedicated analysis of the complete patient-reported outcome data is deferred to a future report
The authors acknowledge the same enrolment bias towards intrahepatic tumours was seen in TOPAZ-1
critique: The absolute gain is 1.8 months of median survival and both supporting efficacy endpoints failed their prespecified boundaries: progression-free survival at HR 0.86 (0.75-1.00), p = 0.023 against a boundary of 0.0125, and objective response at 29% against 29%, p = 0.47

Identical response rates with a survival difference means the drug is not shrinking tumours; the mechanism offered, longer duration of response in the minority who respond, is an observation in a non-randomised subset of responders

The progression-free survival confidence interval ends exactly at 1.00 and the endpoint is declared not met, yet the overall survival claim is presented without the caveat that no intermediate endpoint supports it

The intrahepatic subgroup hazard ratio of 0.76 (0.64-0.91) is the number clinicians quote, but extrahepatic (0.99, 0.73-1.35) and gallbladder (0.96, 0.73-1.26) both cross 1; the trial reports no interaction test and the authors attribute the pattern to underpowering rather than to a site effect, so the subgroup cannot be treated as an iCCA-specific result

Mandatory tumour tissue at entry selected for accessible, biopsiable tumours, which skews the population towards larger intrahepatic masses and away from the patients whose disease is hardest to sample

PD-L1 gave no signal at all, HR 0.84 below a combined positive score of 1 and 0.85 at 1 or more, and with only 10 MSI-high patients there is no biomarker to select on, so 22% of patients incur immune-mediated events for a benefit that cannot be predicted

Treatment-related deaths were higher with pembrolizumab, 8 (2%) against 3 (1%), while all-cause adverse-event deaths were lower, 31 (6%) against 49 (9%); the paper leads with the latter comparison and the attribution of deaths in an unblinded-to-causality assessment is investigator-determined

Quality of life did not improve: the change in EORTC QLQ-C30 global health status to week 18 was -2.5 in both arms, difference 0.0 (-2.5 to 2.6), so the 1.8-month survival gain comes with no measurable improvement in how patients feel

Gemcitabine was continued to progression with no cycle cap, unlike TOPAZ-1, so the two immunotherapy trials are not comparable on chemotherapy exposure and the cross-trial equivalence frequently asserted between them is not supported
495 of 1564 screened patients were not randomised and the reasons are not characterised in the report, so the trial population is a selected 68% of those assessed

The sponsor's employees are co-authors, the sponsor performed the statistical analysis and held the database, and the sponsor funded medical writing; no independent statistical replication is described

Crossover was not permitted and post-progression immunotherapy in the control arm is not accounted for, so the overall survival comparison embeds whatever second-line treatment each region happened to provide
88% of patients had metastatic disease and the trial excluded resectable disease, so it provides no evidence for neoadjuvant, conversion or peri-transplant use of this regimen in liver-confined iCCA

The linked comment by Slater and Cunningham (Lancet 2023;401:1826-1827, PMID 37075782) is listed as the paper's commentary; its full text was not available, so none of its arguments are represented here
37075781.n: 1069 patients randomised from 1564 screened at 175 centres between October 2019 and June 2021 with previously untreated unresectable locally advanced or metastatic biliary tract cancer; 633 (59%) were intrahepatic and 943 (88%) metastatic
37075781.bottom_line: KEYNOTE-966 met its primary endpoint, adding pembrolizumab to gemcitabine-cisplatin for a median survival of 12.7 against 10.9 months, HR 0.83 (0.72-0.95), and it is the larger and longer-followed of the two first-line immunotherapy trials. It does not show tumour-level activity: response rates were identical at 29%, progression-free survival missed its boundary, and quality of life was unchanged. With 88% metastatic disease, a mandatory-biopsy entry criterion that over-selected intrahepatic tumours, and no predictive biomarker, it cannot be read as an iCCA-specific or a liver-confined-disease result.
37075781.funding: Merck Sharp and Dohme, a subsidiary of Merck and Co; authors employed by the funder contributed to design, data analysis, interpretation and writing, and the funder maintained the study database

limitations: No limitations section; the panel records its own uncertainty by grading most surgical and locoregional recommendations at Oxford level of evidence 4, that is retrospective single-centre series

Explicit statements that no recommendation can be provided on resection versus locoregional or systemic treatment when the inferior vena cava, hepatic vein or portal vein is macroscopically involved (88% agreement), on ablative-dose external beam radiotherapy as an alternative to systemic therapy in unresectable liver-limited disease (87%), and on resection to prevent iCCA in hepatolithiasis
The panel notes BILCAP was negative on intention-to-treat and positive only per protocol, and that the ASCOT intrahepatic subgroup was 58 patients with a hazard ratio of 0.75 (0.30-1.89)
The biopsy recommendation is stated to be graded strong despite low-quality evidence, on the grounds that a definitive diagnosis has critical clinical relevance
Each recommendation carries its Delphi agreement percentage, so the panel discloses where agreement was weakest, including 78% for routine FDG-PET and 80% for endoscopic ultrasound nodal sampling
critique: The 3 cm transplant threshold is more permissive than the evidence the guideline cites for it: the international series it rests on studied single tumours of 2 cm or less diagnosed on explant, and its only data above 2 cm is a six-patient post hoc subgroup, so the number in the recommendation appears nowhere in the underlying study as a tested threshold

The same transplant recommendation also requires that the tumour arise in cirrhosis and be early stage, but does not state how a 3 cm iCCA is to be diagnosed before transplantation in a cirrhotic patient, which is precisely what the cited series could not do

Adjuvant fluoropyrimidine is graded a strong recommendation at level 2 evidence on the strength of an iCCA hazard ratio of 0.65 taken from a subgroup of a trial that failed its primary endpoint; the panel reports the failure in its text and grades the recommendation strong anyway

Thermal ablation is suggested for a single tumour under 2 cm while transplantation is permitted up to 3 cm, so the guideline sets a more restrictive size limit on the less invasive treatment without explaining the inconsistency

Delphi agreement is reported but the underlying evidence review was graded by a single panel member before revision, so each level of evidence rests initially on one reader with no stated duplicate assessment or adjudication process

The guideline requires over 75% agreement for a question to be considered at all, which means questions on which the panel disagreed were dropped rather than recorded as uncertain, and the reader cannot see which questions those were

Routine FDG-PET for nodal metastases in apparently resectable patients is a strong recommendation carried at 78% agreement, barely above the threshold, and no sensitivity or specificity figures for PET nodal staging in iCCA accompany it

First-line gemcitabine-cisplatin plus durvalumab is graded level 1 with 100% consensus on a trial that was 86% metastatic with a 1.3-month median survival gain reported at an interim analysis; nothing in the recommendation distinguishes that population from the liver-confined patients the rest of the guideline addresses

Small duct and large duct subclassification is suggested at level 4 or 5, and no recommendation anywhere in the document is conditioned on that subtype, so the classification is endorsed without being made actionable

Conflicts of interest are not printed with the guideline but deferred to separate EASL forms, so a reader cannot see the industry relationships of a 34-member panel making recommendations on durvalumab, FGFR inhibitors and ivosidenib
The document was corrected in September 2023 (J Hepatol 2023;79:1342), with the corrigendum revising the level-of-evidence table, so the grades in the original print differ from the corrected record
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed, so no independent published appraisal of the first iCCA-specific guideline exists in the citation record
37084797.bottom_line: The first guideline written for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma alone, and the source of the positions now quoted in practice: biopsy for diagnosis, MRI and PET for staging, six months of adjuvant oral fluoropyrimidine, gemcitabine-cisplatin with durvalumab first line, and transplantation considered for cirrhotic tumours of 3 cm or less under protocol. Almost all of the surgical and locoregional guidance is level 4 evidence, and the 3 cm transplant ceiling is not a threshold any cited study tested. Where the panel could not agree, it says so, including on vascular involvement and on ablative radiotherapy.
37084797.funding: No funding statement; commissioned by the EASL and ILCA governing boards in 2020, with conflicts of interest not printed in the article but referred to accompanying EASL disclosure forms

limitations: The authors frame the document as guidance rather than protocol, requiring individual patient-centred decisions
They state revision will be needed within five years
They state that the size criteria for transplantation in iCCA need to be monitored and modified to improve recruitment to the national protocol
Searches were completed in November 2022
Several recommendations carry an explicit quality of evidence of LOW, including offering surgery when histology cannot exclude malignancy
Recommendation 46 states that development and funding of clinical trials is key because the pharmacological management of symptoms has not been properly evaluated
critique: Adjuvant capecitabine is a STRONG recommendation on moderate evidence although BILCAP missed significance on intention-to-treat and showed no benefit in its intrahepatic subgroup, so the document's firmest surgical statement rests on a per-protocol result with ACTICCA-1 still unreported

Transplantation for iCCA is routed into a national protocol whose size criteria the guideline simultaneously says need modifying to improve recruitment, which concedes the criteria are set too tightly to be tested while offering no alternative threshold

The two established transplant pathways are left unresolved: neither the very-early cirrhotic tumour nor the locally advanced tumour stable on chemotherapy is given a criterion, so UK practice is directed to a protocol rather than to a decision
Nothing is said about regional lymphadenectomy or a minimum node yield at resection for iCCA, although nodal status determines both stage and the adjuvant decision Recommendation 37 then makes

Recommendation 34 is printed with a quality of evidence of STRONG, a category that does not exist in the GRADE scheme the guideline declares it is using, so at least one of 50 graded recommendations cannot be interpreted

First-line immunotherapy is recommended only conditionally, if approved and available, which makes the central systemic recommendation dependent on local reimbursement rather than on the trial evidence
The November 2022 search closed before KEYNOTE-966, the HER2 data and futibatinib, so a 50-recommendation document published in 2024 describes a systemic landscape that had already changed

Molecular profiling at the earliest opportunity is a STRONG recommendation on high evidence, with a companion recommendation to reserve tissue for it before planning immunohistochemistry; no assay failure rate, panel content or turnaround expectation is given, so the recommendation is strong on process and silent on feasibility

Resection is restricted to high-volume centres with full supporting services as a STRONG recommendation on moderate evidence, with no volume threshold stated, which makes the recommendation unauditable
FDG-PET/CT is recommended for all nodal and distant staging as STRONG on moderate evidence, with no sensitivity, specificity or change-in-management data supplied in the recommendation text

Perihilar transplantation under 3 cm is given a MODERATE recommendation on the basis that it gives long-term disease-free survival, a statement of fact about outcomes rather than a comparison with resection, and the 3 cm figure is carried across to the iCCA discussion by proximity rather than by evidence

No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed; the only linked item is a 2025 Gut letter naming the Guidelines Development Group (PMID 39160057), so no independent appraisal of the recommendations exists in the citation record
37770126.bottom_line: The BSG guidelines are the most operational document in this set for UK practice: 50 GRADE-graded recommendations covering staging imaging, biopsy, high-volume resection, 24 weeks of adjuvant capecitabine, molecular profiling at the earliest opportunity, and iCCA transplantation only inside a national protocol. Its strongest surgical recommendation rests on BILCAP's per-protocol result, it sets no nodal dissection standard while making nodal status decisive, and one recommendation is graded with a category outside the GRADE scheme it declares. The November 2022 search closed before KEYNOTE-966 and the HER2 and futibatinib data.
37770126.funding: The authors declare no specific grant from any public, commercial or not-for-profit funding agency and no competing interests; the guidelines were not commissioned and were externally peer reviewed

limitations: The microwave ablation sample is limited relative to the resection group because so few patients receive ablation for iCCA in real-world practice, although the authors note it is nearly three times the largest previous ablation series and quote a power of 0.996
Ablative and surgical margins were measured by different methods, which the authors accept may introduce bias
The retrospective design carries potential selection bias
Unmeasured confounding and residual confounding from measurement error in confounders, including several variables with standardised mean differences above 0.1 after matching
Stepwise selection in the Cox regression may be subject to estimation bias, and the hazard ratios suffer from built-in selection bias
The authors state ablation may be unsuitable for patients with hepatolithiasis or GGT above 50 U/L, for left-lobe tumours, for patients under 60, and should be used with caution above 3 cm
critique: Equivalence is claimed from a non-significant overall survival hazard ratio of 0.96 (95% CI 0.71-1.29); the upper bound allows a 29% higher death hazard with ablation, no non-inferiority margin was prespecified, and a quoted power of 0.996 is a calculation made on the effect that was observed

The prespecified secondary endpoint went the other way and clearly so: disease-free survival favoured resection, median 1.7 versus 3.6 years, HR 0.63 (0.48-0.83), P = .0010, and this is the result the paper's conclusion sets aside

The equivalence headline comes from a post hoc split at 2017, chosen because ablation case numbers rose after that year, and even in the later era the point estimate still favours resection, HR 0.74 (0.49-1.12), P = .129; a non-significant difference in a smaller subgroup is not equivalence

No adjustment for multiplicity is reported anywhere, although the paper runs two era comparisons, four margin strata and at least six clinical subgroups after a primary analysis that had already been performed

A 5-year disease-free survival of 37.3% is reported for patients treated between 2017 and 2022 in a dataset that closes in June 2022, so that estimate can only be carried by the first year or two of that era and no numbers at risk are given

The denominator narrows twice without explanation of who was lost: 10,441 screened to 944 treated with curative intent within Milan criteria, then 18 ablation patients who matched no resection were discarded, leaving 203 of 221

Margin, the mediator credited with 34.5% of the disease-free survival difference, is contrast CT or MR measured 3 to 5 days after ablation in one arm and direct specimen measurement in the other; the mediation model treats two differently defined quantities as one variable

Conditioning on an ablative margin of 5 mm or more selects the technically successful ablations, because that margin is only known from imaging obtained after the procedure; the resulting parity, HR 0.83 (0.52-1.32) for disease-free survival, is therefore a comparison of successful ablations with all resections

Perioperative mortality is given as 1.5% versus 2.4% with P < .01, which corresponds to roughly 3 deaths against 17 in the matched arms; no test of those proportions yields P < .01, so the stated significance cannot be reproduced from the numbers printed

The entry criterion was Milan-equivalent, a single tumour up to 5 cm or up to three each 3 cm or less, not 3 cm; the paper is nonetheless cited for a 3 cm position, and its only 3 cm finding is that 3-5 cm size was an independent disease-free survival risk factor after ablation but not after resection

Percutaneous ablation yields no specimen and no nodal dissection, so node-negative status in the ablation arm rests on imaging alone in a disease where imaging sensitivity for nodal metastasis is poor, and no pathological node status is available to drive adjuvant decisions

Treatment was assigned by multidisciplinary team and patient preference, and the ablation arm started with more multiple tumours, more bilobar disease and higher comorbidity scores, so the matched comparison is reconstructing a counterfactual from groups that differed on exactly the axes that determine prognosis

All ten centres are Chinese tertiary hospitals with high ablation volume in a population where hepatitis B and hepatolithiasis are common, so neither the complication rate nor the margin achievement rate transfers automatically
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed, so no independent published appraisal accompanies the equivalence claim
38261915.n: 944 patients treated with curative intent within Milan criteria, culled from 10,441 iCCA patients at ten Chinese tertiary hospitals between January 2009 and June 2022: 221 percutaneous microwave ablation and 723 liver resection, reduced to 203 versus 588 after one-to-many propensity score matching
38261915.bottom_line: In 944 patients with iCCA inside Milan-equivalent criteria, microwave ablation gave overall survival indistinguishable from resection with much lower procedural cost and morbidity, provided a margin over 5 mm was achieved. It does not show equivalence: the disease-free survival endpoint favoured resection outright, and the equivalence claim depends on a post hoc split at 2017 whose later comparison is underpowered at P = .129. The entry criterion was a single tumour up to 5 cm, so the study cannot be read as support for a 3 cm rule.
38261915.funding: Funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (92159305, 81971625, 82030047); the funder had no role in design, collection, analysis, interpretation or writing; no interests to report

limitations: No limitations section; the authors concede in the discussion that microsatellite instability status was missing for approximately 50% of patients in each group because of insufficient tissue or an unknown result, and that only 5 of 333 evaluable patients were MSI-high, so a statistical conclusion about that subgroup cannot be drawn
They report that the smoothed hazard function and the log-log plot confirmed a departure from the proportional hazards assumption
They present the survival result as a prespecified interim analysis rather than a final one
critique: This is an interim analysis with 424 of the 496 planned deaths, so the reported hazard ratio is the first look that crossed its boundary, and interim estimates at a crossing boundary are systematically larger than the eventual effect

The absolute difference in median overall survival is 1.3 months, 12.8 against 11.5, which is within the trial's own imaging and follow-up granularity and considerably smaller than the 24-month separation the authors emphasise

With proportional hazards formally violated, the single hazard ratio of 0.80 that carries the registration claim describes no constant effect: the paper's own split shows 0.91 (0.66-1.26) to 6 months and 0.74 (0.58-0.94) afterwards, so early patients derive nothing

The 24-month survival estimates that make the result look large, 24.9% against 10.4%, have confidence intervals of 17.9-32.5 and 4.7-18.8 and come from the thinnest part of the curve at an interim cut; no numbers at risk at 24 months are given alongside them

PD-L1 expression did not predict benefit, 0.79 (0.61-1.00) at tumour area positivity of 1% or more against 0.86 (0.60-1.23) below, so there is no way to spare the 12.7% of patients who had immune-mediated adverse events from an exposure most will not benefit from
Responses were investigator-assessed with no blinded independent central review, in a trial whose response and progression-free survival results are used to support the primary claim

Subgroup point estimates differ substantially, 0.73 in Asia against 0.89 in the rest of the world and 0.49 in locally advanced against 0.83 in metastatic disease, with no multiplicity control and no interaction test reported, so the applicability of the headline to a Western, metastatic population is not established by this trial

86% of patients had metastatic disease and ampullary cancer was excluded, so the trial speaks to palliative treatment of disseminated disease and not to the liver-confined, downstaging or peri-transplant settings where the regimen is now borrowed

Durvalumab continued as monotherapy until progression while gemcitabine-cisplatin was capped at eight cycles in both arms, so the experimental arm receives indefinite treatment and the control arm receives nothing after cycle 8; part of the tail separation may be maintenance of any kind rather than immunotherapy specifically

Only 44% of the cohort had an evaluable microsatellite instability result, so the argument that a hypermutated subset is not driving the signal rests on a biomarker measured in fewer than half the patients

AstraZeneca sponsored the trial, collaborated on the design, collected, analysed and interpreted the data, supplied the drug and paid for the medical writing, and the sponsor vouches for the data alongside the authors; no fully independent analysis is described

No crossover or post-progression immunotherapy accounting is reported, so what the control arm received after progression, which determines how much of the overall survival difference is attributable to first-line durvalumab, cannot be assessed
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed for this report, so no independent published appraisal accompanies it
38319896.n: 685 patients randomised from 914 enrolled at 105 sites in 17 countries between April 2019 and December 2020, with previously untreated advanced biliary tract cancer; 383 of 685 (55.9%) had intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and 86% had metastatic disease
38319896.bottom_line: TOPAZ-1 is the trial that added immunotherapy to first-line gemcitabine-cisplatin in advanced biliary tract cancer, with a hazard ratio of 0.80 (0.66-0.97) and 24-month survival of 24.9% against 10.4%. The median gain is 1.3 months, the result is an interim analysis at 424 of 496 planned deaths, and the proportional hazards assumption is formally violated, so the single hazard ratio summarises a benefit that begins only after six months. With 86% metastatic disease and no predictive value from PD-L1, it says nothing about liver-confined disease or about which patients should be exposed.
38319896.funding: Funded by AstraZeneca, which sponsored the trial, collaborated on design and on the collection, analysis and interpretation of the data, supplied durvalumab, co-ran the analyses with PHASTAR, and funded the medical writing

limitations: The study design included no active comparator treatment arm
Small numbers in the patient subgroups limit interpretation of efficacy by demographic and disease characteristics
The authors refer the reader to the earlier primary report for the trial's other limitations rather than restating them
They note that routine comprehensive genomic profiling is needed to find patients who might benefit, and that the first-line role of FGFR inhibition remains for FIGHT-302 to establish
critique: With no comparator, a 37.0% response rate and 17.5-month median survival cannot be separated from the biology of FGFR2-fusion disease, which the paper itself states carries longer survival from diagnosis than FGFR2-wild-type cholangiocarcinoma

The headline response rate fell from 35.5% in the 2020 primary report to 37.0% here on a differently sized cohort (108 against 107), and the two figures are quoted interchangeably in the literature without noting that the denominator changed

Cohorts B and C are 20 and 17 patients with zero responses, so the clean negative result the paper relies on to define the biomarker is a weak negative that cannot exclude a response rate of 10% or more
Only 12 of 40 responders (30.0%) responded for 12 months or longer and 12-month progression-free survival was 32.3%, so two-thirds of patients had progressed within a year

Every patient had a treatment-emergent adverse event, 68.7% grade 3 or worse and 46.3% serious, with dose interruption in 42.2% and discontinuation in 10.2%; this is a demanding drug and the abstract characterises the events as manageable

The TP53 hazard ratio of 3.33 (1.48-7.52) and PBRM1 hazard ratio of 2.46 (1.24-4.87) are exploratory co-alteration analyses in a 108-patient cohort with no multiplicity adjustment, offered as prognostic findings

Acquired kinase-domain resistance mutations arose in all patients who responded and then progressed, which means the benefit is intrinsically time-limited, and the paper's conclusion emphasises durability

Incyte funded the trial, paid for the writing and employs three authors who hold shares, and the paper's own conclusion is that the results further support the regulatory approvals of Incyte's drug based on this single-arm study

107 of 108 cohort A patients had intrahepatic disease, so despite being titled a cholangiocarcinoma study the result applies to iCCA only, and the second-line-or-later setting means nothing here speaks to perioperative or conversion use
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed for this final analysis, so the only critical reading available is internal to the text
38838500.n: 147 patients with previously treated advanced or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma at 146 sites in 12 countries, assigned by central FGF/FGFR status to cohort A with FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements (108), cohort B with other alterations (20) and cohort C with none (17); 90% had intrahepatic disease and 107 of 108 in cohort A were intrahepatic, with median follow-up of 42.9 months in cohort A

The whole document was written by two authors with ESMO committee review, so the evidence selection rests on two readers and no search strategy, date range or inclusion criteria are reported

Molecular profiling is recommended at level I, grade A at the start of first-line therapy for a panel of eight gene targets, without any statement of the expected yield, the assay failure rate or what to do when profiling fails, which in biliary specimens is common
The futibatinib and pemigatinib recommendations carry ESMO-MCBS scores of 3 and 2 from single-arm trials where the magnitude-of-benefit scale has no comparator to score against

Hepatic arterial infusion and selective internal radiotherapy are relegated to supplementary material with no graded recommendation, so the liver-directed options that matter most in liver-confined iCCA are effectively removed from the update

Nothing is added on resection, adjuvant therapy, nodal staging or transplantation, so the update modernises only the systemic half of the parent guideline while being cited as the current ESMO position overall

The DESTINY-PanTumor02 response rate of 56.3% quoted for trastuzumab deruxtecan comes from an immunohistochemistry 3+ subgroup of a pan-tumour basket trial, and the number of biliary patients behind it is not given in the update

Triplet chemotherapy is rejected on two negative randomised trials while the one positive Japanese triplet is reported without a recommendation either way, leaving the reader with a geographically split evidence base and no guidance
Both authors declare advisory and speaker relationships with the manufacturers of the recommended agents, in a document whose entire content is which drug to give
Small duct intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is singled out as enriched for actionable targets, but no recommendation is conditioned on that subtype and no prevalence figures by subtype are given
No linked editorial or comment was found in PubMed, so no independent published appraisal accompanies the update
39864891.bottom_line: This interim update brings the ESMO biliary tract cancer guideline up to date on molecular diagnostics and advanced disease: profile at the start of first-line treatment, add either durvalumab or pembrolizumab to gemcitabine-cisplatin, avoid triplets, and use futibatinib, pemigatinib, HER2-directed agents, NTRK and RET inhibitors by alteration. Nearly all of it is level III evidence graded A, so strong recommendations rest on single-arm and basket-trial data, and the two HER2 recommendations depend on an assay the same document says cannot be specified. It is silent on surgery, adjuvant therapy, staging and transplantation.

No breakdown by anatomical subsite is reported anywhere, so the effect in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma specifically is unknown even though HER2 testing is now done on iCCA

Pain is the only patient-reported outcome, measured at two time points on a single Brief Pain Inventory item, and the comparison is between responders and progressors rather than between treatments, so it describes what responding to treatment feels like and not what the drug does

41264278.n: 80 patients with ERBB2-amplified locally advanced or metastatic biliary tract cancer previously treated with gemcitabine-based chemotherapy, enrolled between September 2020 and March 2022, 62 with immunohistochemistry 3+ and 18 with 2+ tumours, followed for a median of 33.4 months

limitations: The repeat liver resection group remains small because so few patients undergo repeat resection in real-world practice
Potential selection bias persists because of the design, despite propensity score matching and overlap weighting
Hepatic function preservation and quality of life, the outcomes most relevant to a minimally invasive treatment, could not be measured

Unmeasured and residual confounding from measurement error in confounders, and stepwise selection in the Cox models that may bias the estimates

critique: Similarity is inferred from three non-significant hazard ratios for overall survival, 0.89 (0.68-1.17), 0.88 (0.67-1.15) and 0.97 (0.73-1.30); no non-inferiority margin was set, so the confidence intervals admit up to a 30% higher death hazard with ablation and the paper's own 4-month median gap sits inside them

Disease-free survival at HR 0.78 (0.61-1.00), P = .07 has an upper bound touching exactly 1.00 and is reported as similar; in the matched set it is 0.81 (0.62-1.06), so the one endpoint that measures local control is consistently directional against ablation and never excluded

The paper is presented as a secondary analysis of a prospective cohort yet its own limitations paragraph attributes the selection bias to the retrospective design, so the reader cannot tell which parts of the data were collected prospectively

18.0% of participants, 89 of 494, were lost to follow-up and censored at last contact, 18.4% in the ablation arm and 16.8% in the resection arm, on top of 42 excluded for lost follow-up at screening; losses of that size in a survival comparison of this margin are not addressed in the analysis

Four subgroups are reported in which repeat resection beat ablation for disease-free survival, each with a confidence interval that approaches 1 (0.32-0.91, 0.52-0.98, and two at roughly 0.65 with P = .02 and .046), with no multiplicity adjustment stated for the subgroup set

Treatment was chosen by multidisciplinary team and patient preference and the imbalance was large before weighting, including tumour number with a standardised mean difference of 0.38 and P < .001; the overlap weighting that drives the standardised mean differences towards zero also reweights the population away from the patients clinicians actually had to choose for

E values of 7.26 and 6.79 are quoted as evidence of robustness to unmeasured confounding, but an E value this high simply reflects a hazard ratio close to 1; it is not evidence that no confounding was present

Repeat resection carried 31.3% major complications against 5.5% for ablation, yet 119 patients were still selected for it, which implies the resection arm was chosen for fitness and the two arms were never exchangeable on operative candidacy

The ablation arm has no specimen from the recurrence, so large duct versus small duct subtype, the strongest prognostic factor reported here, is classified from the original resection rather than from the recurrent tumour being treated

All ten centres are Chinese tertiary hospitals and operators had a median of 10.5 years of independent ablation experience, so a 5.5% major complication rate and the margin achievement behind these results should not be assumed to transfer

Entry was Milan-equivalent, a single recurrence up to 5 cm or up to three each 3 cm or less, with mean tumour size 2.7 cm; the study therefore says nothing about recurrences beyond those limits, which is the larger share of recurrences in practice

41528222.n: 494 patients with a first intrahepatic recurrence of iCCA within Milan-equivalent criteria, selected from 10,441 screened in the MALRIC cohort across ten Chinese tertiary centres from January 2009 to June 2024: 375 microwave ablation and 119 repeat liver resection
41528222.bottom_line: At a first intrahepatic recurrence of iCCA within Milan-equivalent limits, microwave ablation produced overall survival statistically indistinguishable from repeat hepatectomy with a sixth of the major complications and a quarter less cost. It does not establish equivalence: median survival was 4 months shorter, disease-free survival was directionally worse with an upper bound exactly at 1.00, and four prespecified strata favoured repeat resection. Eighteen percent of the cohort was censored for lost follow-up, and the authors themselves call the results exploratory.

critique: The comparison that carries the paper, 82% against 44% sensitivity, is between tests run on different specimens; the authors' defence is the size of the gap and the size of the cohort, which is an argument from magnitude rather than a controlled comparison

FISH, the adjunct actually used in primary sclerosing cholangitis, was never compared directly because the data were not collected, and the paper instead argues against FISH on the grounds that it does not identify genes or actionable targets, which is not a sensitivity comparison
EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration, the alternative for distal strictures, was also not compared, so the test is positioned against the weakest available comparator

A stricture could be classified as neoplastic on imaging plus 12 months of clinical or radiographic progression rather than on tissue, so the reference standard partly incorporates the work-up the positive test triggers, which inflates sensitivity

Specimens were submitted at the endoscopist's discretion rather than consecutively, so this is not a consecutive series and the prevalence of 56% neoplastic strictures reflects referral and submission behaviour rather than any defined population
5% of patients had no follow-up and were dropped from the accuracy analysis without characterisation, and these are the patients whose strictures were least likely to be resolved

Only 2% of neoplastic strictures were purely dysplastic, so outside primary sclerosing cholangitis this is earlier detection of established cancer rather than early detection, and no survival, resectability or stage-shift benefit is demonstrated anywhere in the paper

The clinical-utility claim rests on 56 patients whose management changed, of whom 37 (66%) had stable disease or a response by RECIST; stable disease as the endpoint in an uncontrolled series cannot distinguish treatment effect from natural history

All testing was done in the single laboratory that developed the assay despite 28 contributing institutions, so the multi-institutional design applies to specimen collection and not to assay performance

Two assay versions with very different content, 28 genes and 167 fusions against 161 genes and 763 fusions, are pooled into one sensitivity figure, and the actionable-alteration yield is reported for v3 only, so neither number describes a single test

Sixteen false positives occurred with variant allele frequencies from 1.5% to 30%, including KRAS, TP53, GNAS and CTNNB1, and at a 1.5% allele frequency the distinction between a false positive and a sampling-limited true positive is not resolvable from the data presented
The actionable-alteration figure differs between the abstract (20% of v3-positive neoplasms) and the body (23%, 188 of 812), and the discrepancy is not explained
The senior author declares honoraria from Foundation Medicine and Olympus in a paper recommending routine sequencing of endoscopically obtained biliary specimens

41905432.bottom_line: Across 2116 patients at 28 institutions, DNA and RNA sequencing of ERCP specimens detected neoplastic strictures with 82% sensitivity and 98% specificity against 44% and 99% for pathology, rising to 88% combined, and for intrahepatic or hilar strictures the gap is 80% against 36%.
